title: A Hierarchical Multi-Task Framework for Dementia Diagnosis via Pathological Feature Learning from Multi-Organ Data
reviewer_1_strengths: The authors integrate four public datasets and further construct a private clinical cohort, resulting in a large-scale multi-center dataset for evaluation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.For the cognitive staging task, the paper compares the proposed method with ResNet18, ViT, ADRD, and MoMmNet-B. However, the current baseline setup remains insufficient. First, the paper lacks strong baselines that can effectively exploit and fuse multi-organ information. Second, regarding the confounder removal emphasized by PFD, the paper does not compare against other plausible debiasing or confounder-handling strategies. 2.In Table 2, the classification results for co-occurring etiologies are reported only for two combinations, namely AD+LBD and AD+FTD. The manuscript does not explain why only these two mixed-etiology categories are included. It remains unclear whether these are the only co-occurring etiologies present in the dataset, or whether other combinations were excluded for methodological or data-availability reasons. 3.The description of the PFD module remains insufficiently clear. In particular, Figure 2(d) suggests that subjects in certain age ranges, such as 40–50 and 90–100 years, are relatively sparse. Since PFD relies on NC subjects within matched demographic profiles to estimate the mean and variance, the number of available reference samples may become quite limited in these underrepresented groups, especially considering that not all subjects are labeled as NC. The manuscript should therefore clarify whether each matched demographic profile contains a sufficient number of NC samples for robust estimation, and how the method handles cases in which adequately matched reference samples are unavailable. 4.Although the implementation details state that missing modalities are represented by zero vectors, it would be important to clarify whether alternative strategies for handling missing modalities were considered or evaluated, and whether the reported results remain consistent under different missing-modality handling schemes.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper models dementia as a systemic, multi-organ disease and handles co-occurring etiologies via multi-label prediction. 2.The study uses a large cohort aggregated from multiple sources, which increases generalizability.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Limited Justification of Feature Alignment: Feature Alignment is only applied to FDG and DXA modalities, while other modalities are not aligned. The rationale for choosing these modalities and excluding others is not clearly justified. 2.Missing comparisons with modern multimodal fusion architectures (e.g., cross-attention transformers). 3.Several details are unclear: dimensionality of feature representations, exact architecture of fusion (ViT configuration), memory bank implementation details. The hierarchical training procedure is only briefly described.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The framework successfully broadens the scope of traditional neuroimaging analysis by incorporating multi-organ and multi-modal data, establishing a more holistic brain-body axis for disease evaluation. The PFD module is an elegant engineering contribution. By dynamically updating the NC feature memory bank at every epoch to perform real-time normalization within the latent space, the architecture effectively forces the model to isolate and focus on purely pathological features.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.While the authors claim that the PFD module successfully mitigates demographic and biological confounders, the paper lacks rigorous empirical evidence to substantiate this. Further qualitative and quantitative validation (e.g., specific correlation analyses or feature space visualizations) are needed to definitively prove that the decoupled representations strictly encapsulate only pure pathological characteristics without any residual confounding effects. 2.For etiology prediction, the relatively lower performance in non-AD groups suggests potential challenges in capturing heterogeneous pathological patterns across different etiologies. 3.The evaluation was limited to 5-fold cross-validation without external validation, which may restrict the generalizability of the model to independent datasets. 4.The requirements for multi-organ data may limit the practical applicability of the proposed framework, as such comprehensive datasets are rarely available in routine clinical settings. 5.The proportion of missing modalities was not explicitly reported, and missing data were represented as zero vectors. This approach may introduce ambiguity, as the model cannot distinguish between truly absent data and valid zero-valued features, potentially leading to biased representations and reduced robustness.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. We summarize our responses into five main themes. 1) PFD Validity and Data Sparsity (R1, R2, R3) PFD differs fundamentally from conventional adversarial debiasing. Its goal is to quantify latent features as deviations from healthy baselines. As reported in Table 3, adding PFD alone improves NC vs. MCI vs. DE classification accuracy from 0.683 to 0.719, demonstrating its ability to suppress age-related confounders while enhancing pathology-related signals. For sparse age groups (e.g., 40–50 or 90–100 years), we acknowledge that the implementation details were insufficiently described in the manuscript. In the submitted implementation, we adopt a dynamic sliding-window expansion strategy to ensure a minimum number of NC samples (e.g., N=30). When an age bin contains insufficient samples, adjacent age ranges are symmetrically expanded until the threshold is reached, thereby enabling stable estimation of demographic-specific statistics. 2) Baselines and Experimental Completeness (R1, R2) Regarding modern multimodal fusion architectures, our evaluation already includes ADRD (Xue et al., Nature Medicine, 2024), a recent transformer-based multimodal framework for dementia diagnosis. Together with ResNet-18 and ViT backbones, our experiments provide a comprehensive evaluation across both conventional deep learning architectures and recent multimodal fusion strategies. Direct comparison with existing multi-organ methods remains difficult because current studies are limited and typically designed for specific organ combinations. To address this in our manuscript, we first evaluated a brain-only version of our framework (MoMmNet-B) against existing brain-based multimodal methods to validate the proposed architecture. We then compared MoMmNet with MoMmNet-B to directly quantify the contribution of peripheral-organ information. 3) Missing Modality Handling (R1, R3) Prior to submission, we compared zero-vector and random-padding strategies for handling missing modalities, consistently observing superior performance with the zero-vector approach. Within our framework, this strategy is not merely an engineering choice but a clinically grounded prior. Since PFD quantifies latent features as physiological deviations from healthy-control baselines, a zero-vector naturally corresponds to the average healthy physiological state, providing a stable and biologically meaningful padding representation. Regarding the concern that zero vector padding may introduce ambiguity between missing modalities and valid features, this scenario is highly unlikely in practice. Although individual feature dimensions may be zero, a complete 512-dimensional representation cannot realistically collapse into an exact zero vector. Therefore, the model can reliably distinguish missing modalities from valid representations. 4) Rationale for Modality-Specific Feature Alignment (R2) Feature Alignment (FA) is applied exclusively to FDG and DXA because these are the only modalities that contain both brain and peripheral-organ imaging information. In contrast, all other modalities are limited to brain imaging alone. Since the primary objective of FA is to align peripheral-organ representations into a brain-centered feature space, this module is only required for FDG and DXA. 5) Co-occurring Etiology Selection (R1) We focused on AD+FTD and AD+LBD because they are among the most clinically prevalent mixed-dementia patterns involving AD. As shown in Fig. 2, these are also the only mixed-etiology groups with sufficient sample sizes to support reliable method training and evaluation. Therefore, we selected these two mixed-etiology settings for co-occurring dementia evaluation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper models dementia from a systemic multi-organ and multi-etiology perspective. The construction of a large multi-center cohort and the integration of brain, heart, gut, liver, kidney, and clinical text information are clear strengths. However, the experimental comparison is not yet sufficiently convincing. The paper lacks strong modern multimodal fusion baselines, such as cross-attention transformer-based methods, and does not compare PFD against other plausible debiasing or confounder-removal strategies. This makes it difficult to assess whether the proposed modules are truly necessary. Several key methodological claims need stronger support. The PFD module is claimed to remove demographic and biological confounders, but the paper does not provide enough quantitative or qualitative evidence to show that the learned features are truly pathology-specific. The handling of missing modalities by zero vectors is also underexplored and may introduce ambiguity or bias. | The rebuttal reasonably clarified the main concerns about PFD implementation, feature alignment, missing-modality handling, and mixed-etiology selection. I support acceptance, but the authors should clearly address in the camera-ready version the remaining concerns on limited baseline coverage and the weakened demographic-matching assumption of PFD under sparse age groups. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reading the authors’ rebuttal, I recommend acceptance. The paper addresses an important and clinically meaningful problem by modeling dementia diagnosis from a systemic multi-organ and multi-etiology perspective. The integration of brain, heart, gut, liver, kidney, and clinical text information in a large multi-center cohort is a clear strength, and the proposed hierarchical framework is well aligned with the complexity of dementia diagnosis. The rebuttal satisfactorily clarified several of my major concerns. In particular, the authors explained the rationale and implementation of the PFD module, including the use of demographic-conditioned healthy-control reference features and the dynamic sliding-window strategy for sparse demographic groups. Although this strategy may not fully eliminate all concerns regarding confounder removal, it provides a reasonable and practical solution. The authors also clarified the missing-modality handling strategy, the reason why Feature Alignment is applied only to FDG and DXA modalities, and the selection of co-occurring etiologies based on clinical prevalence and available sample sizes. I still believe that the paper would benefit from stronger comparisons with additional modern multimodal fusion and debiasing methods, as well as more direct evidence that the learned representations are truly pathology-specific. However, these limitations do not fundamentally undermine the contribution. Overall, the paper presents a novel and clinically relevant direction for multi-organ dementia modeling, supported by a large-scale dataset, coherent methodology, and reasonable rebuttal clarifications. I therefore consider the work to be above the acceptance threshold. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a hierarchical multi-task framework for multi-organ and multi-etiology data analysis from dementia diagnosis. The reviewers’ critiques were mainly related to performance evaluation using state-of-the-art multimodal fusion methods, clarification of the PFD module, and clarification of experimental settings, such as classification results for co-occurring etiologies. While those are important aspects, the rebuttal addressed them sufficiently and the paper maintains its novelty.

title: Asym-MSF: Asymmetric Multi-scale Structural Fusion for Robust BCVA Prediction with Self-supervised Fidelity Constraints
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper has several strengths. First, the core motivation is clinically reasonable and well-matched to the application. Treating OCT as the primary structural modality, while using SLO and text as auxiliary context, is a sensible assumption for BCVA prediction and provides the method with a clear design rationale. Second, the proposed framework is not just a straightforward fusion variant. The asymmetric latent bottleneck uses OCT-derived queries to compress auxiliary information in a targeted way, which is more thoughtful than standard symmetric fusion. The dynamic modulation design further enhances the conditioning’s adaptability and task specificity. Third, the self-supervised restoration branch is a meaningful component. It aims to regularize the modulation process so that auxiliary information does not distort the underlying OCT structure, a relevant consideration in medical imaging settings. Fourth, the empirical results on the reported dataset are promising. The method improves MAE over the compared baselines, and the ablation results are generally consistent with the paper’s main narrative. In particular, comparing different foundational modalities supports the choice of OCT as the anchor modality. Finally, the paper is fairly easy to follow at a high level. The main idea is clear, the overall framework is intuitive, and the anonymized code link is a positive sign for reproducibility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The main weakness of the paper is that the experimental evidence is still insufficient to support the scope of its claims. The method is evaluated on a single clinical dataset using a random 8:1:1 split, without external validation, cross-center testing, or clarification on whether the split is performed at the patient level. Since the dataset contains 2,141 eyes from 1,960 patients, this detail is important, as non-patient-level splitting could lead to overly optimistic results. A second concern is that the paper strongly emphasizes robustness to missing modalities, yet this is not validated in a sufficiently direct way. Although the manuscript states that SLO is missing in about 63% of cases, it does not provide controlled experiments under different missingness settings, stratified analyses by missingness pattern, or comparisons between complete and incomplete cases. It is therefore difficult to determine whether the gains truly come from better handling of missing or noisy auxiliary data. The paper also lacks computational analysis. Given the complexity of the proposed framework, including the asymmetric bottleneck, dynamic kernel generation, spectral gating, and restoration branch, it would be important to report parameter counts, FLOPs, runtime, or memory usage. Without such analysis, the practical cost of the method remains unclear. In addition, the method description is not fully self-contained. Some important implementation details are either only briefly mentioned or deferred to prior work, which leaves gaps in reproducibility. The related-work discussion could also be stronger, particularly in positioning the method against broader literature on missing-modality learning and reliability-aware multimodal fusion. There are also several presentation issues, including inconsistent notation in Fig. 1 and inconsistent acronym expansions in Table 2, which reduce clarity. Finally, the evaluation is somewhat limited, with Accuracy quickly saturating and no variance estimates or statistical testing reported. Overall, the idea is interesting, and the results are promising, but the current evidence is not yet sufficient to fully justify the strength of the claims.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Well-motivated clinical problem formulation：The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of prior multimodal BCVA prediction methods, namely the use of symmetric fusion despite an inherent hierarchy among modalities. The argument that OCT should be treated as the structural anchor, while SLO and text should play supporting roles, is clinically intuitive. The proposed method achieves the best performance among all compared methods, outperforming both the strongest baseline UML and the DyKen-Hyena architecture.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the overall framework is well assembled, several components are conceptually related to existing ideas: the bottlenecked cross-attention resembles Perceiver-style compression, the dynamic kernel generation builds upon prior dynamic-kernel formulations, and the self-supervised restorer uses reconstruction-based regularization with gradient/frequency constraints. As a result, the main novelty seems to lie more in the asymmetric clinical formulation and the integration of existing ideas than in a fundamentally new modeling primitive. Limited validation scope. The authors emphasize that the method preserves anatomical fidelity and filters noisy auxiliary signals, but these claims are mostly supported indirectly through performance improvements.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper introduces a well-motivated asymmetric fusion paradigm that aligns with clinical priors, effectively addressing noise contamination and modality incompleteness by prioritizing OCT as a structural anchor. 2.The proposed multi-scale dynamic modulation mechanism is technically sound and capable of capturing complex anatomical structures at different granularities, improving representation quality. 3.The integration of self-supervised fidelity constraints helps preserve structural consistency and leads to strong empirical performance on real clinical data.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.I suggest the authors ensure that the symbols used in the figures are consistent with those in the textual descriptions, as this would improve clarity and make the method easier to follow. 2.The paper claims to address the issue that symmetric fusion may contaminate pristine OCT features with auxiliary noise. However, this problem appears to be directly handled only by the SFR module. I recommend revising this statement for better alignment with the method. Additionally, the ablation study lacks results for using the SFR module alone. 3.In the methodology section, it would be helpful to explicitly state that Asym-MSF is designed for Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA) prediction, which would improve overall readability and understanding. I look forward to seeing an extended journal version of this work
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and Meta-Reviewer for their constructive feedback. Q1: Missing/noisy auxiliary modalities. (R1, Meta) A1: We study real clinical missingness: OCT/text are routinely available, while SLO is absent in ~63% of cases. Asym-MSF therefore anchors on OCT and uses SLO/text as auxiliary context. It improves over UML in this setting (MAE 0.0457→0.0378; Acc 96.25%→98.60%). Controlled dropout, which artificially masks auxiliary modalities in complete cases to simulate missingness rates, was not used as main evidence because it would rely on the smaller complete-modality subset and may introduce selection bias. We will revise the claim to real-world SLO missingness, not exhaustive robustness to all missingness patterns. Q2: Validation scope and split protocol. (R1, Meta) A2: Only 181 eyes (8.5%) in our dataset share patient identity with another eye, so patient-level overlap is limited. This eye-level protocol is also consistent with prior BCVA prediction studies [1,2]. External validation was omitted because no comparable clinical dataset with the same multimodal inputs and postoperative BCVA labels is available. All baselines and Asym-MSF used the same split, preprocessing, and metrics, so the relative gains are unlikely to arise from protocol differences. We will clarify the protocol and avoid overstating patient-independent or cross-center generalization. Q3: Computational cost. (R1, Meta) A3: Asym-MSF has 34.19M training parameters and 28.88M active inference parameters, since SFR is training-only, compared with 27.20M for UML. Its inference complexity is 5.17 GFLOPs/sample versus 4.40 for UML, a 17.6% increase. Although moderately heavier, Asym-MSF improves MAE from 0.0457 to 0.0378 and Acc from 96.25% to 98.60% over UML. Since postoperative BCVA prediction is not a real-time task, this trade-off is practical. We will report these implementation-derived statistics and clarify the training/inference distinction. Q4: Method clarity and presentation. (R1, R3) A4: We will improve the self-contained description of ALB/DCM/SFR, explicitly state that Asym-MSF is designed for postoperative BCVA prediction, and fix notation/acronym inconsistencies in figures and tables. Q5: SFR role and ablation. (R3) A5: We will clarify that auxiliary-noise mitigation comes from ALB, DCM, and SFR jointly, not SFR alone. ALB filters auxiliary evidence with OCT-derived queries, DCM injects it via controlled modulation, and SFR regularizes DCM-generated kernels to preserve OCT anatomical fidelity. Because SFR depends on DCM-generated kernels, an “SFR-only” setting is not a valid standalone model; therefore, we evaluate SFR by comparing the full model with its no-SFR variant. Q6: Novelty and relation to existing ideas. (R2) A6: Our contribution is an OCT-anchored asymmetric fusion design for BCVA prediction, using reliable OCT structure to guide potentially incomplete/noisy SLO-text context. ALB differs from [3] by generating spatial-aware seeds from OCT features, so SLO/text are compressed according to OCT anatomy rather than modality-agnostic tokens. DCM differs from [4] by replacing the MLP-based kernel generator with multi-branch dilated convolutions to model multi-scale structural patterns. Together with SFR, these modules leverage auxiliary information while preserving OCT structure. Our comparisons and ablations support the contribution of this asymmetric design. [1] Incomplete Multimodal Learning for Visual Acuity Prediction After Cataract Surgery Using Masked Self-Attention. MICCAI (2023). [2] UML: A Unified Multimodal Learning Framework for Cataract Postoperative Visual Acuity Prediction with Uncertain Missing Modalities. ICASSP (2025). [3] Perceiver IO: A general architecture for structured inputs & outputs. ICLR (2022). [4] DyKen-Hyena: Dynamic Kernel Generation via Cross-Modal Attention for Multimodal Intent Recognition. arXiv (2025).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses a clinically important problem with a well-motivated asymmetric fusion design. One reviewer recommends Accept (5), one Weak Accept (4), and one Weak Reject (3). The main concerns center on limited validation (single dataset, no external validation, unclear patient-level splitting), lack of controlled experiments for missing-modality robustness, and missing computational cost analysis. These concerns are addressable during rebuttal. Given the strong support from Reviewer 3 and the clinical relevance of the problem, the paper should proceed to rebuttal with a clear expectation that the authors address the validation and robustness concerns. | The paper proposes a well-motivated asymmetric multimodal fusion framework for BCVA prediction, anchored on OCT with auxiliary SLO/text inputs, which aligns well with clinical practice. Reviewer #3 gave Accept (5), Reviewer #2 gave Weak Accept (4), and Reviewer #1’s Weak Reject (3) raised concerns about validation scope and computational cost—issues that were adequately addressed in the rebuttal. The overall consensus supports acceptance, and the core methodological contribution remains solid. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes Asym-MSF, an asymmetric multimodal fusion framework for postoperative BCVA prediction that prioritizes OCT as the structural anchor while incorporating auxiliary modalities for refinement. Reviewers agreed that the problem is clinically important and that the asymmetric fusion design is well motivated. The method demonstrates promising performance improvements on a real clinical dataset. The main concerns raised during review included limited validation scope (single dataset, no external validation), insufficient direct experiments for missing-modality robustness, lack of computational cost analysis, and several presentation issues. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified the split protocol, contextualized the missing-modality setting using real-world clinical missingness, provided parameter/FLOPs analysis, and better explained the roles of ALB, DCM, and SFR. The rebuttal also clarified the methodological novelty and appropriately moderated several claims. Importantly, Reviewer #1 updated their score from Weak Reject to Weak Accept after rebuttal, while the other reviewers maintained positive assessments. Overall, the paper presents a clinically meaningful and technically sound contribution with convincing empirical results despite some remaining limitations in validation scope. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After reading the rebuttal and other reviewers’ comments, I think the authors have provided reasonable clarifications to the reviewers’ concerns.

title: Boundary-Aware Multi-Granularity Learning for Depression Severity Estimation
reviewer_1_strengths: The idea of using continuous predictions with ordinal classes are interesting and not much studied. Their proposed loss function is meaningful. State-of-art results ranging from notable to significant in different datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: No mention of the input modalities (face, voice. . . ) is a shortcoming. In general, Fig 3 can be improved (remove Mamba encoder detail, and focus on the flow). Variables/dimensions may be used for clarity and redundancy about loss terms can be removed. Datasets can be a little described for people not working in this same problem.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S1.Novel and well-motivated methodology: The multi-granularity supervision framework addresses a real clinical problem - that standard regression treats all prediction errors equally, regardless of whether they cross clinically meaningful severity boundaries. The combination of MSE, OCR, and PSCL is, to the best of this reviewer’s knowledge, novel for depression severity estimation. S2.Comprehensive comparison: The paper compares against 20 methods across four standard benchmarks (AVEC 2013, AVEC 2014, DAIC-WOZ, E-DAIC), covering visual-only, audio-only, and multimodal settings. State-of-the-art performance is achieved across virtually all configurations. S3.Rigorous ablation and statistical testing: The ablation study systematically removes each component and includes Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, paired t-tests, and bootstrap confidence intervals - exceeding the statistical rigour normally provided. S4.Theory-to-practice validation: Theorem 1 is empirically validated in Figure 4, where OCR loss peaks at the clinical thresholds as predicted. This connection between theoretical motivation and experimental evidence strengthens the paper’s narrative. S5.Additional analyses: The paper includes hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, Grad-CAM interpretability visualisations showing clinically relevant facial regions, and detailed component analysis of the contrastive learning module, providing a thorough understanding of the method’s behaviour.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1.Insufficient related work and baseline descriptions: The related work section discusses only two prior depression estimation methods, yet Tables 1 and 2 compare against 20 methods. The paper would benefit from briefly describing the key baselines, particularly the closest competitors (e.g., DepMGNN, FC-AEN, SIMMA), so the reader can understand what approaches the proposed method improves upon and why. Additionally, CORAL and SORD are discussed as motivation but not included as explicit experimental baselines. Given that the competing methods are not described, it is unclear whether any of them already employ ordinal regression approaches, making it difficult to assess whether the proposed method’s advantage comes specifically from the multi-granularity formulation. W2.Clarity and accessibility: The paper is difficult to follow for readers outside the area. The paper would benefit from a clearer description of the overall pipeline beyond the architecture diagrams. The input modality, preprocessing steps, and model architecture are largely left to be inferred from figures rather than described explicitly in the text. The four evaluation datasets are named but not described (number of subjects, recording conditions, label distributions). The evaluation protocol (e.g., whether the standard challenge partitions were used) is not explicitly stated. Readers unfamiliar with these benchmarks would need to check the original challenge papers to verify that comparisons are conducted under identical conditions. A few sentences describing the end-to-end pipeline, datasets, and evaluation protocol would significantly improve accessibility for the broader MICCAI audience. W3.No limitations discussion: The paper does not discuss any limitations of the proposed approach. A brief limitations paragraph in the conclusion would strengthen the paper.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The theoretical justifications for the methodologies presented strengthen the contribution. The authors also establish state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets for depression severity. The paper was well written, with key contributions made clearer using diagrams. Overall, the methods could be valuable for automated severity assessment, beyond the domain of depression.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My main feedback concerns the decoupling of the model from the optimization process. It is not clear which one is the primary contributor to SOTA performance. Is it achieved via task-specific modeling, such as using carefully curated audio and video feature extractors and Mamba encoders? Or is it because of the loss functions and regularizations introduced by the authors? It would further strengthen the study if the authors could examine what happens if the same (or similar) architecture is trained with simply MSE loss MSE loss + multi-class classification loss or other ordinal classification losses used in the literature The authors mention comparing against several baselines. But ideally, one would want to show and separate the effects of the introduced loss function. Some minor feedback: In Abstract: “This granularity mismatch leads to boundary-agnostic optimization and unstructured representations.” – unstructured representations sound a bit vague, especially when, in the abstract, the readers do not know what type of structure you are talking about. Figure 2: Raw Input -> Are both top and bottom labels “Video”, or one should be “Video” and another should be “Audio”?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Dear Area Chair and Reviewers, We sincerely thank the reviewers for their careful reading, thoughtful evaluation, and highly constructive comments. We are truly encouraged by the positive feedback and deeply appreciate the time and expertise dedicated to improving our work. We will faithfully address all concerns in the camera-ready version. Our detailed responses follow. Q1.Architecture vs. loss contribution and ordinal-classification objectives [R3, R2-W1]. We sincerely thank R3 for this insightful question, which goes to the heart of our contribution. The ablation in Table 3 directly addresses the relative contribution of architecture and optimization. With the Mamba backbone fixed, moving from MSE-only to PSCL, OCR, and the full objective consistently reduces MAE on AVEC2013 and AVEC2014, validated by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, paired t-tests, and bootstrap CIs. This confirms measurable gains from the proposed losses without changing the backbone. We fully agree with R3 that head-to-head comparisons against alternative ordinal losses under the same backbone would further isolate our objective’s contribution, and we gratefully take this excellent suggestion as a valuable direction for future work. Regarding CORAL and SORD, we will clarify their conceptual difference: they reformulate regression as ordinal classification, whereas our method preserves continuous regression and introduces ordinal information only as regularization, without altering the task formulation. Q2.Input modalities, pipeline, datasets, and evaluation protocol [R1, R2-W2]. We deeply appreciate R1 and R2 for this perceptive suggestion, which will substantially enhance the readability and reproducibility of our paper. In the Datasets and Implementation paragraph, we will clarify that experiments cover visual, audio, and audio-visual settings: visual inputs use HOG+SVM face features and audio inputs use STFT-based log-Mel features. We will also describe the four benchmarks, namely AVEC2013/2014 (BDI-II, 0–63) and DAIC-WOZ/E-DAIC (PHQ-8, 0–24), with severity thresholds and official splits. Q3.Related work and baselines [R2-W1]. We are very grateful to R2 for this constructive suggestion, which will strengthen the positioning of our work. We will explicitly position the closest competitors, including DepMGNN, FC-AEN, SIMMA, PointTransform, and AVA-DepressNet, as point-wise regression methods without explicit ordinal supervision, which is the gap our method addresses. CORAL and SORD will be described as ordinal-classification approaches that discard continuous scores. As they produce discrete grades rather than continuous BDI-II/PHQ-8 outputs, they are not directly comparable under our regression metrics (MAE/RMSE); we will make this explicit in §2.All revisions will remain within §2.Q4.Limitations [R2-W3]. We sincerely thank R2 for this valuable suggestion, which will further improve the rigor of our paper. We will add a concise statement in the conclusion noting that our evaluation relies on public benchmarks with limited scale and diversity, and that broader validation across larger and more diverse cohorts remains future work. Q5.Figures and wording [R1, R2, R3]. We greatly appreciate the reviewers’ meticulous attention to figures and wording. In the camera-ready version, we will: (i) correct Figure 2 by labeling the lower “Raw Input” branch as “Audio”; (ii) replace “unstructured representations” with “ordinally unstructured representations”; and (iii) following R1’s suggestion, streamline Fig. 3 by reducing internal Mamba details to highlight the overall flow, and trim redundant descriptions of loss terms. We again sincerely thank the reviewers for their careful reading and constructive suggestions. These targeted revisions will improve the clarity, rigor, and value of the paper for the MICCAI community.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers recommend acceptance, with strong consensus on the paper’s merits: a novel and clinically meaningful multi‑granularity supervision framework, state‑of‑the‑art results across four benchmarks, and exceptional experimental rigor including thorough ablations and statistical testing. Minor concerns, such as the need for clearer baseline descriptions, disentangling the contribution of the loss functions from the architecture, are addressed in a revision. Overall, the paper makes a solid and valuable contribution. Conclusion: Early Accept.

title: CalibSleep: Cross-Modal Calibration and Rule-Aware Learning for Automatic Sleep Stage Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper proposes the CalibSleep, a dual-branch cross-modal calibration fusion framework, for the automatic sleep staging task. By leveraging bidirectional cross-attention to achieve semantic alignment of heterogeneous features in the time and time-frequency domains, combined with adaptive calibration and AASM rule-aware phase transition regularization, it effectively improves the physiological consistency and classification performance of sleep staging. Extensive experiments on both the in-house dataset and the public SHHS1 dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The CMC module proposed in this paper achieves semantic alignment through bidirectional cross-attention and uses an adaptive weight α to balance time-domain and time-frequency-domain features. However, only the overall effectiveness of the CMC module is verified via ablation experiments; the individual contributions of bidirectional attention and adaptive calibration are not decomposed, making it impossible to clarify their independent effects on performance improvement. 2.The comparative experiments in this paper only cover several unimodal and time-frequency multimodal baselines, without including high-performance sleep staging methods based on Transformer and graph neural networks in recent years. 3.The specific design of the AASM transition matrix and the sensitivity of the hyperparameter λtrans are not elaborated, nor is the improvement of regularization on each sleep stage quantitatively analyzed.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The integration of physiological priors via a rule-aware transition loss provides a biologically meaningful constraint to the classification process without relying on complex long-range sequence modeling. The dual-stream architecture effectively captures both temporal and spectral dynamics making good use of modal complementarity. Furthermore the experimental results on both an in-house clinical dataset and the public SHHS1 dataset demonstrate strong empirical performance and reliable generalization capabilities.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: While the CalibSleep framework demonstrates solid empirical performance, its architectural novelty is somewhat limited. The model primarily relies on a combination of established neural network components, such as the standard stack of CNN, SENet, and BiGRU for the time-domain encoder, and the existing TimesNet for the time-frequency branch. The cross-modal calibration module also utilizes standard cross-attention and a gating mechanism. Although this combination is effective, it represents more of an engineering integration rather than a fundamental methodological innovation in multi-modal deep learning. Additionally, integrating these multiple modules may introduce extra computational overhead, but the paper lacks a detailed analysis of parameter counts and inference latency which are important for clinical deployment. Finally, including comparisons with more recent transformer-based or graph-based state-of-the-art models would further strengthen the demonstration of the proposed method’s absolute superiority.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The most striking strength of this paper is the elegant design of the rule-aware transition loss. Instead of employing computationally expensive long-range temporal models (such as large Transformers or deep RNNs) to implicitly learn transition probabilities, the authors ingeniously inject clinical rules directly into the objective function. By calculating the transition matrix of adjacent single-epoch predictions and penalizing unlikely shifts, the model captures essential temporal context and clinical consistency in a highly lightweight and effective manner.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Robustness of Rule-Aware Loss Against Label Noise: While theoretically appealing, the practical utility of the rule-aware loss requires further justification, specifically regarding the inherent ambiguity of sleep stage transitions. Sleep transitions are notoriously fuzzy, and even highly experienced clinicians often disagree when annotating these boundary epochs. For instance, as detailed in the dataset paper “ISRUC-Sleep: A comprehensive public dataset for sleep researchers”, inter-rater disagreement between expert scorers can be as high as 20%. Given that the ground-truth labels themselves contain significant noise during transitions, enforcing a rigid physiological prior matrix might over-penalize the model or force it to learn hard boundaries that do not reflect the continuous nature of human sleep. The authors need to discuss whether this explicit signal remains effective in the presence of such high inter-rater variability. Lack of Statistical Significance Testing: The quantitative results presented in Tables 1 and 2 report absolute metrics (ACC, MF1, Kappa) but completely omit standard deviations or confidence intervals. Because the performance margins between the proposed method and some baselines (or among ablation variants) are relatively narrow, it is impossible to determine whether these improvements are statistically significant or merely the result of favorable random seeds. To convincingly prove the method’s effectiveness, the authors must conduct multiple runs to report standard deviations and perform appropriate statistical significance tests (e.g., t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests).
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the constructive comments and for recognizing CalibSleep’s design, evaluation, performance, and clinical interpretability. Following MICCAI rebuttal policy, we do not introduce new/additional results, but clarify the submitted evidence and acknowledge limitations where new experiments would be required. Novelty and positioning. We agree that several low-level encoders use established components. Our contribution is not the isolated use of CNN/BiGRU/TimesNet/cross-attention, but the formulation of sleep staging as calibrated integration of temporal and time-frequency evidence under physiological transition constraints. Unlike simple concatenation or one-way attention, CMC performs bidirectional semantic querying between domains and learns an epoch-adaptive calibration gate alpha to balance temporal and spectral reliability. Fig. 3(a) supports this design: alpha shows meaningful stage-dependent behavior, emphasizing time-domain EOG-related evidence in Wake/REM and spectral evidence in N1-N3. Component contribution and transition prior. Table 2 evaluates the proposed components: compared with dual-stream concatenation (0.836/0.833/0.828 ACC/MF1/Kappa), adding CMC improves performance to 0.872/0.846/0.841, and further adding rule-aware regularization yields 0.896/0.877/0.874.We agree that the manuscript should better disentangle sub-component roles: bidirectional attention handles cross-domain alignment and feature conflict; adaptive calibration performs sample-wise evidence weighting; Lcalib stabilizes feature consistency during training; and Ltrans penalizes physiologically implausible adjacent-epoch predictions. M encodes adjacent-stage rationality according to AASM-guided sleep evolution knowledge. Ltrans is a probability-weighted soft regularizer, not a hard constrained decoder. lambda_trans=0.1 balances this prior with cross-entropy: lambda_trans=0 degenerates to ordinary classification, while an overly large value may over-constrain ambiguous transitions. Baselines, computation, and deployment. We apologize that the baseline positioning was not sufficiently clear. Table 1 includes representative unimodal, time-frequency, multimodal, and Transformer-related methods, including SFormer/SleepTransformer and MultichannelSleepNet variants, as well as XSleepNet, SleepBoost, CoReSleep, and CrossFusionSleepNet. We acknowledge that additional GNN comparisons and parameter/latency profiling would further strengthen the paper. Qualitatively, the physiological priors are deployment-friendly: the contrastive calibration loss and transition loss are used only during training and introduce no extra inference-time decoder. CalibSleep operates on 30-s EEG/EOG epochs and does not require whole-night self-attention or graph construction. Statistical rigor and robustness. We agree that reporting mean/std and significance tests would improve empirical rigor, and we will explicitly discuss this limitation. Nevertheless, the submitted evidence is not limited to one narrow setting: CalibSleep shows consistent gains on the in-house No.6 dataset and external SHHS1 dataset, across ACC/MF1/Kappa, ablation variants, and interpretability analyses. Robustness to label ambiguity. We fully agree that boundary epochs are ambiguous and inter-rater disagreement exists. Our rule-aware loss does not assume deterministic transitions or override expert labels. It acts on the predicted transition probability p_{t-1}p_t^T and softly discourages implausible transitions, while cross-entropy from manual annotations remains the primary supervision. Thus, ambiguous epochs can still be determined by signal evidence. Fig. 3(b,c) suggests that the regularizer mainly suppresses physiologically unlikely confusion, such as N3-REM, rather than blindly smoothing predictions. We hope these clarifications address the concerns on novelty, component roles, baselines, practicality, statistical rigor, and robustness.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a dual-stream framework for automatic sleep stage classification. The reviewers acknowledged the model design, extensive experiments, improved performance, and clinically meaningful interpretability. This paper’s significant would be better highlighted if the authors address several important points raised by the reviewers, such as clarifying the methodological novelty, positioning the work relative to stronger recent baselines (through proper background review), disentangling the contributions of the proposed calibration components, reporting variance and statistical significance, discussing computational cost, deployment practicality, and robustness. | The rebuttal seems to have clarified the intended role of the calibration and rule-aware components and to have preserved a positive overall stance after rebuttal, even though some requests for stronger contextualization and significance analysis remained. Because the core contribution is useful and the main concerns appear manageable rather than fatal, I support acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal addressed the major reviewer concerns satisfactorily, particularly regarding the positioning of the contribution, the role of the calibration components, the interpretation of the rule-aware transition regularization, and the practical deployment considerations. The authors also clarified the rationale behind the architectural design and acknowledged the limitations regarding additional statistical analysis and computational profiling. The paper presents a technically sound and clinically meaningful framework for automatic sleep stage classification. The integration of cross-modal calibration with physiologically guided transition regularization is well motivated and supported by strong empirical performance on both in-house and public datasets. The rule-aware transition loss provides an elegant and lightweight mechanism for incorporating clinical sleep transition priors without requiring heavy long-sequence modeling. I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers found the paper clinically motivated and empirically strong. After rebuttal, the main concerns on novelty, baselines, efficiency, and statistical validation were sufficiently addressed, supporting acceptance.

title: CURA: Calibrated Uncertainty with Retrieval and Agents for Trustworthy Multimodal Medical Decision Support
reviewer_1_strengths: The tasks are defined nicely, with the three different scenarios. The study on council (table 3) motivates the choice of having several agents in the design. The method is extensively evaluated.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: I think the paper might benefit a lot with a more extensive set of baselines. It is not clear why only a fixed 500-question subset is used for selective abstention study. In table 3, it seems that the single expert is pareto-optimal and adding experts lowers the accuracy. Although briefly discussed, it is still not clear if the added experts are less accurate or what the problem is. Do different experts make different mistakes or the failures are correlated? A more detailed ablation on the system’s components is missing and it is not clear which components are contributing to the model’s performance.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Clinically relevant topic. The field has shown that multi-LLM/multi-agent setups can be helpful, but it is unclear whether “more is better”, and with several AI “opinions”, it becomes important to explore aggregation techniques - quantifying and utilizing uncertainty for aggregation is worth exploring, especially for us in the medical field. Clean experiment setups (e.g. withholding evaluation/benchmark datasets from the KG resources) Adaptive council evaluation is insightful. Finding that blind scaling of experts degrades calibration is valuable for the community Insightful evaluation on multiple benchmarks, including VQA-RAD for multimodal context
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Related works section is very short - too short imho, to provide a sufficient overview of the current state of the art in multi-LLM belief aggregation or multi-agent deliberaton (uncertainty-based or not). Only 6 works are cited in “Related Work”, and 3 of which ([15,29,30]) deal with grounding, not aggregation, i.e. they don’t really “count”. The authors claim the experts report an answer with “calibrated confidence” (c_i). However, these are raw, self-reported LLM probabilities (i.e. literally, an output token describing the LLM’s “confidence” in its own opinion). Self-reported LLM confidences are not “calibrated” (LLMs are non-deterministic) and often prone to overconfidence. While the final system output might be calibrated via conformal prediction, referring to the individual input scores c_i as “calibrated” without applying an actual calibration technique is incorrect and misleading terminology throughout the paper. Math formulation for Bayesian Belief Aggregation uses an exact equality, but the normalization term is missing from the log posterior equation. Probably, softmax was used and posteriors were normalized anyway (which is not reflected in the formula) - if posteriors are not normalized though, the entropy calculation would be meaningless because the probabilities would not sum up to 1.- Independence assumption in Bayesian aggregation is not discussed. LLM/Agent “experts” built on similar base LLMs likely have highly correlated errors Evaluation leans heavily on multiple-choice questions, but clinical practice often requires open-ended reasoning. VQA-RAD results are included but limited in depth The organization of the paper is good (apart from too short Related Works), but the clarity is medium. The paper obviously had to be crammed into 8 pages, but it is also written in an extremely complex way. For a future revision (e.g. towards journal extension) I would wish for authors to be a bit clearer in the way they describe their motivations, methods and outcomes, and using some intuitive explanations. I find it hard to read papers that suffer from “academic obfuscation”, and this paper is leaning somewhat in that direction.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This paper is well organized and easy to follow.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My main concern is its limited novelty; mostly a combination of existing methods. Agent design is not well justified. A simpler agent-based approach may be more effective than the proposed council. Comparison is a bit weak; as far as I know, some SOTA approaches are not included in Table 2.So the current results are not that convincing.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for the careful reading. We address the main cross-cutting concerns below. Novelty and positioning (R1,R3,MR). Rather than a standalone debate protocol or a claim that larger councils are always better, CURA contributes a reliability-centered framework in which one aggregated posterior serves as a single interface for answer fusion, selective abstention, split conformal sets, uncertainty-gated escalation, and interactive information gathering. Compared with prior debate/council work, the focus is posterior-level reliability, not debate mechanics. With same-backbone specialists, blind scaling can degrade both accuracy and calibration. CURA therefore includes both a single-specialist mode and uncertainty-triggered escalation; the operating policy is uncertainty-governed rather than council-size-driven. Baselines, simpler agents, and ablation logic (R1,R3,MR). The benchmark table provides context across representative biomedical LLMs, medical RAG methods, and GPT-4.1; the agent-design claim is supported by controlled same-backbone comparisons. Plain GPT-4.1 vs. CURA is the end-to-end pipeline comparison. Single-specialist CURA vs. fixed/adaptive councils compares deliberation size and escalation policy with grounding and the answer interface held constant. In VQA-RAD, baseline vs. expert panel/debate compares multimodal deliberation, with panel gains concentrated in open-ended questions (91.1% to 97.8%), supporting deliberation when the answer space is less specified. Abstention/conformal overlays also act on the same posterior rather than adding learned prediction modules. These submitted controls address the simpler-agent concern: on well-specified MCQ benchmarks, single vs. Fixed-7 is 77.3%/0.058/1.4k vs. 72.7%/0.122/15.6k on MedMCQA and 90.8%/0.052/2.0k vs. 90.4%/0.119/20.4k on MedQA (acc/ECE/tokens), supporting deliberation as a conditional resource rather than a default. Confidence terminology and Bayesian formulation (R2,MR). We agree with this terminology concern: expert-level c_i denotes a self-reported confidence signal used by the aggregator, not an individually calibrated probability. System-level reliability is evaluated via ECE/risk-coverage, while split conformal prediction provides the formal marginal coverage guarantee under the usual calibration/test exchangeability assumption. For the Bayesian equation, the intended computation is an unnormalized log-posterior score: ell_k = log(1/K) + sum_i w_i log P(o_i|y=k), p_k = exp(ell_k) / sum_j exp(ell_j); entropy and conformal prediction use p_k. Dependence among experts (R1,R2,MR). Specialist personas diversify prompting, but they are not statistically independent evidence sources when sharing a backbone. Additional same-backbone experts can propagate correlated errors, so more opinions need not improve MCQ performance. The aggregation uses a conditional-independence approximation, not a claim about true error independence. Split conformal coverage applies to the final predictor and does not require independence among internal experts. 500-question subset and evaluation scope (R1,R2). The fixed seeded 500-question subset is used for reliability/operating-point analyses, keeping risk-coverage sweeps and the 250/250 split-conformal calibration/test protocol matched across operating points. The main QA accuracy results are reported on the benchmark evaluation splits. The KG/retrieval store excludes benchmark datasets and official explanations/answer keys, reducing retrieval leakage. Because single, fixed, and adaptive CURA variants share the same backbone, benchmark exposure alone is unlikely to explain their relative behavior, especially larger-council degradation. The claims are aligned with the evaluated settings: MCQ QA, VQA-RAD multimodal QA, and interactive diagnosis.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers raise consistent concerns regarding limited novelty, insufficient baseline comparisons and ablation studies, and unclear experimental design choices (e.g., subset selection and multi-expert behavior), which require stronger justification. In addition, several methodological aspects need clarification and correction, particularly the use of “calibrated confidence,” the Bayesian formulation, and the independence assumption among LLM experts, as these affect the theoretical soundness of the approach. The authors are encouraged to use the rebuttal to clarify these points, provide additional experimental evidence (e.g., ablations, stronger baselines), and better position the work within existing multi-agent aggregation literature to support the paper’s claims. | The paper is accepted, as the reviewers agreed that, despite limited methodological novelty, the work is interesting, technically sound, and provides a meaningful basis for future research. The rebuttal satisfactorily addressed several important concerns regarding posterior normalization, confidence terminology, and expert correlation assumptions. Overall, the paper was viewed as a worthwhile and discussion-worthy contribution for the conference community. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper presents CURA, a multimodal medical decision-support framework that combines retrieval, clinical-agent aggregation, Bayesian belief fusion, and reliability overlays such as abstention and conformal prediction. While the framework may have potential clinical utility, the overall contribution appears to be mainly a combination of existing techniques rather than a clearly novel methodological advance. In addition, the experimental study design does not appear sufficiently strong to support the paper’s claims, especially given the fast-moving nature of this area and the need for rigorous validation in clinical decision-support settings. As a result, the paper is not yet ready for acceptance at MICCAI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have clearly positioned their focus on posterior-level reliability beyond existing debate-based works and clarified their claims with substantiating ablations and baselines. Most reviewers have acknowledged the merits of the work, in together with its good quality of writing.

title: From Trajectories to Phenotypes: Disease Progression as Structural Priors for Multi-organ Imaging Representation Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: The core idea of borrowing structural knowledge from large-scale longitudinal EHR data to guide imaging predictors is well-motivated and practically useful. The framework is evaluated across a large number of diseases with a carefully partitioned cohort design that attempts to prevent information leakage. The comparison of different alignment objectives provides useful insight into how distillation loss choice affects downstream performance for classification versus time-to-onset prediction tasks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The major concern is a potential information leakage issue that undermines the fairness of the comparison, particularly for the fusion model. Since the fusion model directly uses each evaluation subject’s own pre-imaging trajectory embedding, the model may already have direct access to prior diagnosis of the disease being predicted or closely related comorbidities. A fair evaluation would require predicting only diseases with first onset strictly after the imaging visit. In addition, I have some concerns regarding the disagreement of IDP similarity and trajectory similarity (Fig. 3). Despite the positive correlation, the IDP similarity is very low while the trajectory similarity is generally above 0.8.Also, the confidence interval in fig 3b is not consistent with Fig. 3a, where IDP similarity spans a much wider range at any given trajectory similarity. This result to some extent challenges the claim that imaging and trajectory representations share a common latent disease manifold. Finally, several methodological details including the specific imaging modalities, organ systems, and IDP selection criteria are never clearly stated.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel Method: Using ICD trajectory embeddings as structural priors is an interesting formulation, and the authors show that it helps learn embeddings from IDPs which boost prediction performance on disease forecasting, especially in low-prevalence disease. This could be a useful paradigm even outside of this context, in the larger scope of learning with asynchronous modalities recorded at different time resolutions. 2.Experimental designs are sound and rigorous, with the baselines of IDPs and trajectory embeddings providing meaningful context to interpret their results. 3.Post-hoc analysis of disease-wise gains in AUC is further informative.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The “shared latent manifold” hypothesis for IDP and disease trajectories is hard to digest. While I understand the intuition, I am not convinced that the experiments and results support the claim. The spearman of 0.166 on the permutation test on pairwise IDP and trajectory embeddings is significant, however the following could be confounders: a. Age, BMI, Sex: Controlling for these in the experiment would give a stronger support for the shared latent manifold theory, since these could be potential confounders that cause similar embeddings in both spaces. This is because, as I understand it, the claim is that the disease progression trajectory and IDP share a common latent manifold (independent of demographics). If this is not the claim, then could the authors please clarify? b. The InfoNCE Alignment objective: The embeddings are learned by aligning projections of the embeddings using contrastive learning. This alignment might be driving the pairwise similarity, in which case the effect is a result of the training strategy not a natural phenomenon. It would be more meaningful to do the same experiment but on the non-pretrained embeddings [as a suggestion for future work]. 2.Unclear Writing: Some parts of the paper could be rewritten for clarity. [See Comments below] 3.Missing Discussion of Limitations, Related Work and Future Work: I understand that the authors show extensive experiments, and there is an 8-page limit, but there is no discussion of related work on predicting disease progression on IDPs, or disease trajectories, or even mention of related technical works [Contrastive Representation Distillation, ICLR 2020]. Most importantly, there is no discussion of limitations or implications for use in future research, which is important for any reader trying to interpret these results.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Clean experimental design to prevent subject and temporal leakage Intuitive and interesting motivation for using temporal trajectories to enrich static IDPs
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Some central claims are only supported by weak correlations, making the evidence less convincing. Experiments are conducted on a single dataset (UK Biobank) and mainly compare internal variants.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Dear Area Chair and Reviewers, We sincerely thank all reviewers for the constructive feedback and positive assessment of our work. We are encouraged that the reviewers found the proposed trajectory-aware distillation framework interesting and potentially useful for MICCAI. Our primary goal is to evaluate whether longitudinal disease trajectories can provide useful structural priors for multi-organ IDP representation learning under realistic imaging-cohort constraints, rather than to claim definitive evidence for a universal disease manifold. Leakage and Prediction Setting (R1, Meta-review) We agree that the evaluation protocol should be clarified more explicitly. Our downstream prediction setting follows an incident-only risk-set design with imaging as baseline. For each target disease, subjects with diagnosis onset at or before imaging are excluded as prevalent cases, and positives therefore correspond only to incident post-imaging cases. Controls are sampled from subjects who had already undergone imaging and remained event-free at the corresponding case time. Thus, the task is future-onset prediction after imaging rather than current-state classification. To further prevent temporal leakage, trajectory embeddings used for distillation and downstream fusion are computed only from diagnosis records strictly prior to imaging acquisition. In addition, the downstream IDP-only and fusion pipelines explicitly exclude target-derived variables such as label and delta_time from the feature set, with runtime leakage checks. We will revise the manuscript to make this protocol explicit and easier to follow. Shared Structure Claim (R1, R2, R3) We agree that our current evidence should not be framed as definitive proof of a shared latent disease manifold. The observed alignment between IDP and trajectory similarity is statistically significant but modest, and should be interpreted as preliminary empirical evidence consistent with partially aligned disease-relevant structure. We will moderate the relevant wording accordingly. Baselines and Scope (R3, Meta-review) Our design isolates the effect of trajectory-informed priors through controlled comparisons across IDP-only, trajectory-only, and fusion settings, rather than through an exhaustive benchmark. We agree that the absence of broader comparisons to EHR and multimodal methods is a limitation of the current study. In our formulation, models such as BEHRT and Med-BERT can also be viewed as alternative trajectory encoders/teachers rather than only downstream baselines, and exploring such alternatives is an important direction for future work. Methods (R1, R2, R3) We will clarify the problem formulation, the Delphi trajectory-teacher objective, and the role of trajectory-aware distillation in the Methods more clearly. We will also expand the IDP description: the 301 quantitative phenotypes cover five system-level groups, namely brain MRI grey-matter volumes, skeleton/body-composition measures, cardiac MRI traits, abdominal MRI traits, and pulmonary measures including spirometry and lung volume. The IDP baseline operates on concatenated IDPs, whereas the organ-aware variants group features by organ and aggregate them by concat, weighted pooling, or a transformer. Overall, we will revise the manuscript to (1) make the leakage-prevention and evaluation protocol fully explicit, (2) reduce overclaiming regarding manifold-sharing interpretations, (3) improve methodological clarity and model taxonomy, and (4) strengthen discussion of limitations, external validation, alternative trajectory models, and future directions. We thank the reviewers again for their thoughtful comments and suggestions.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Overall all reviewers found this manuscript presents a useful and interesting algorithm for MICCAI. I am recommending this manuscript for acceptance. Authors in the final version of the manuscript, I recommend addressing the information leakage (R1) and limitations of the comparison methods (R3).

title: Fusion-E2Pulse: A Multimodal Event-RGB Fusion Network for Non-contact Pulse Wave Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated fusion logic The work accurately exploits the physical complementarity between event cameras (high sensitivity to subtle pulsations) and RGB cameras (stable structural periodicity). The design directly targets the core bottlenecks of single-modal non-contact pulse monitoring, with clear clinical and technical value. Sound network architecture The dual-stream encoder avoids premature modal interference; the attentional fusion bottleneck adaptively balances noise suppression and detail preservation, which is well-suited for physiological signal characteristics. Innovative time-frequency adversarial supervision Different from conventional time-domain GANs, the frequency-domain discriminator focuses on physiological periodicity, and the composite loss effectively optimizes both heart rate accuracy and waveform morphology. Ablation studies verify the necessity of each loss component.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Unresolved cross-site timing bias RGB is captured from the face while event streams are from the wrist, introducing Pulse Transit Time (PTT) error. The paper does not model or calibrate this systematic bias, which affects morphological accuracy. Insufficient generalization validation Experiments are only conducted on the EMPD dataset. No cross-dataset testing, no evaluation under challenging conditions (large motion, varying illumination, different camera hardware), so the clinical robustness is unproven. Lack of real-time deployment analysis Inference speed, computational complexity (FLOPs/Params), and edge-device feasibility are not reported, which is critical for clinical real-time monitoring applications. Missing comparison with SOTA baselines The paper only conducts comparisons with traditional rPPG algorithms (CHROM, ICA, POS) and a simple event-only network, but does not compare with any advanced deep learning-based methods for rPPG or pulse wave reconstruction (e. g. , PhysNet, RhythmFormer, PulseGAN).
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Well-motivated multimodal formulation: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of standard camera-based pulse reconstruction by arguing that RGB sensing smooths subtle pulsatile dynamics, while event cameras can capture finer changes but are more fragile to noise and motion. The proposed fusion of RGB structural priors with event micro-dynamics is intuitive and clinically relevant for waveform reconstruction, especially when the goal goes beyond scalar HR estimation toward morphology recovery. Clear architecture and pipeline design: The overall method is easy to follow. Figure 1 on page 3 clearly presents the two-stage design, including preprocessing for both modalities, dual encoders, attentional fusion, decoder, and the frequency-domain discriminator. The roles of the main modules are well separated, and the description of event preprocessing and RGB signal extraction is sufficiently concrete to understand how the final inputs are constructed. Good emphasis on waveform morphology rather than HR alone: A notable strength is that the paper does not reduce the task to heart-rate estimation only. In addition to MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and HR correlation, the authors evaluate waveform correlation, SNR, systolic and diastolic phase duration, and pulse width. This is appropriate for a pulse reconstruction paper whose stated aim is to preserve subtle landmarks such as the dicrotic notch. The waveform examples in Figure 3 and the morphology metrics in Tables 1 and 2 strengthen this aspect of the work. Useful ablation over losses and fusion variants: Table 2 provides a reasonably informative ablation over adversarial, spectral, and morphological losses, and also compares different RGB priors, namely CHROM, ICA, and POS. This helps support two central claims: first, that adversarial training alone is insufficient, and second, that multimodal fusion improves over event-only reconstruction. Strong empirical performance within the presented setup: Within the EMPD benchmark and the baselines considered, Fusion-E2Pulse appears consistently strong. The best fusion variant achieves lower HR error than the event-only model and far better results than the RGB-only priors, while also improving waveform-level measures. The record-split evaluation is especially useful because it attempts to test generalization across samples rather than only within-record continuity.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main limitation is that the experimental comparison is too restricted for the scope of the claims. The paper compares against event-only and classical RGB-derived signals such as CHROM, ICA, and POS, but it does not compare against stronger learned rPPG or waveform-reconstruction approaches such as PhysNet, RhythmFormer, PulseGAN, or other recent deep models discussed in the paper itself. Since the manuscript claims state-of-the-art performance, the absence of direct comparison to modern learning-based baselines makes that claim difficult to assess. The RGB branch is not learning directly from raw video in the same way as many modern RGB-based baselines. Instead, it uses pre-extracted signals from CHROM, ICA, and POS as structural priors. This is a reasonable design choice, but it also means the comparison against RGB-only methods is somewhat asymmetric. The fusion system benefits from a learned reconstruction model on top of both modalities, whereas the RGB-only baselines are classical signal-processing outputs rather than comparably expressive learned models. This weakens the strength of the empirical conclusion that the proposed approach is broadly superior. All experiments are conducted on EMPD, which is valuable and multimodal, but still represents a single benchmark with a specific acquisition setup. Given that the method depends on coordinated RGB, event, and contact-PPG data, external validation is understandably difficult, but the lack of evaluation on another dataset or under clearly distinct conditions makes it hard to judge robustness across devices, skin tones, motion patterns, or illumination regimes. The paper combines several familiar ingredients: dual-stream encoding, attention-based fusion, adversarial learning, Soft-DTW, STFT-based loss, and classical rPPG priors. The overall combination is sensible and appears effective, but the architectural novelty at the module level is limited. The main contribution is better characterized as a careful multimodal integration of existing ideas for a less-explored sensing setup than as a fundamentally new modeling framework. Important implementation and protocol details could be clearer. The paper gives the main optimizer settings and loss weights, but several details remain underspecified for full assessment and reproducibility. For example, the exact event aggregation strategy, ROI localization robustness, preprocessing sensitivity, sequence lengths used during training, and details of how the discriminator input is normalized or parameterized are not fully elaborated. Since the method relies heavily on preprocessing and modality synchronization, more detail would improve confidence in reproducibility. The paper is motivated by cardiovascular screening and waveform morphology, but the experiments stop at signal-level reconstruction metrics. There is no downstream validation showing that the reconstructed waveforms improve clinically meaningful tasks such as disease stratification, arterial stiffness assessment, or reliable dicrotic-notch localization under realistic deployment conditions. This does not invalidate the work, but it does mean the clinical relevance remains indirect.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novelty: the proposed Fusion-E2Pulse architecture is novel, as the literature contains no other works that specifically fuse RGB and event camera information for rPPG. This is only possible because of the EMPD dataset, which this work utilizes, and whose architecture the proposed method is largely based upon [1]. Strong evaluation protocol: the work uses a comprehensive suite of evaluation metrics for both HR estimation and pulsatile signal morphology and provides useful baseline comparisons, enabling rigorous comparison with related work. Thorough ablation study: the authors conduct a strong ablation study (sec 3.3) that helps understand the impact of the different loss components in the final proposed training objective. References: [1] Feng, Q., Li, P., Gao, R., Jiale, X., Gong, R., Li, Y.: Empd: An event-based multimodal physiological dataset for remote pulse wave detection (part 1 of 9) (Feb 2026). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18765701
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Incremental novelty: while the proposed method is novel, it is largely identical to the architecture proposed by the original work that developed the EMPD dataset [1]. In particular, the proposed event preprocessing is identical to the event aggregation module of the original work, and the adversarial pulse reconstruction stage largely resembles the waveform reconstruction module of the original work.
