author_feedback: We thank the Meta-Reviewer (MR) and all reviewers for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that MR recognized our motivation and emphasis on waveform morphology. Below we address the “decisive concerns.” 1.Clarification on Data Partitioning and Robustness (MR, R3) To address the MR’s concern regarding potential data leakage and to clarify the inaccuracies in the assessment of our framework’s robustness, we provide a detailed statistical verification of the model’s performance under a protocol where the training, validation, and test sets are strictly non-overlapping at the subject level. By presenting the metrics under this strictly subject-disjoint partition (58 training, 8 validation, 17 testing), we clarify that the core findings are not artifacts of the record-level split. In this subject-independent view, the architecture maintains a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.73 bpm, a Pearson correlation coefficient ($r_w$) of 0.919, and a Systolic Peak Duration (SPD) error of 17.56 ms. This clarification verifies that the proposed fusion mechanism’s performance, as reported in the manuscript, stems from its genuine generalization capability across unseen individuals rather than data overlap. 2.Comparison with Stronger Learned Baselines (MR, R1, R2) We acknowledge the broad use of “SOTA” and will adopt more precise terms like “advanced” in the final version to better reflect our method’s standing within the specialized multimodal Event-RGB fusion paradigm. The baselines (CHROM, POS, ICA) were selected as physiological structural priors for our fusion framework rather than for direct competition with all frame-based deep learning methods. Given the unique sensing advantages of asynchronous event streams over standard cameras, we focus on the marginal gains in morphological fidelity provided by the fusion mechanism. 3.Novelty vs. EMPD Dataset Paper (MR, R3) We clarify the distinction between this submission and the foundational EMPD work. The EMPD paper focuses on the dataset release and a baseline for HR estimation. This work (Fusion-E2Pulse) addresses the much more challenging task of high-fidelity waveform reconstruction. The technical novelty lies in: 1) The Attentional Fusion Bottleneck, which adaptively calibrates dual-modal weights to suppress event noise while preserving RGB structural priors. 2) The time-frequency adversarial framework using Soft-DTW, which is to enable the recovery of subtle biomarkers like the dicrotic notch. As shown in our new ablation results, the full model outperforms single-modal methods in waveform correlation. 4.Single Dataset and Incremental Gains (MR, R3) Due to unique hardware requirements, EMPD is currently the only available benchmark for this modality. However, our rigorous subject-independent evaluation mitigates this limitation. Regarding “incremental gains” (R3), we acknowledge the observation regarding the modest numerical improvement in HR MAE. However, we emphasize that Fusion-E2Pulse is designed for waveform reconstruction rather than simple HR tracking. While single-modal methods can estimate pulse frequency, they often fail to recover fine-grained morphological landmarks. Our fusion paradigm achieves higher waveform correlation, which is essential for advanced pulse wave analysis. Finally, we clarify that the camera-ready version will explicitly acknowledge current limitations, including the single-dataset dependency and the necessity for further clinical validation, to ensure a balanced and rigorous presentation of our findings.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This is a technically coherent and potentially useful methodological paper on multimodal non-contact pulse wave reconstruction, but the current evidence leaves the submission in a genuinely borderline position. The paper’s main strengths are the clear motivation for combining RGB structural priors with event-camera dynamics, an architecture that is consistent with that motivation, and an evaluation that appropriately considers waveform morphology rather than reducing the task to heart-rate estimation alone. The ablation study is also helpful in showing the contribution of the loss components and the effect of different RGB priors. Within the presented setup, the method consistently improves over the included single-modal baselines. The decisive concerns relate to the scope and interpretation of the empirical evidence. After checking the manuscript, the baseline suite is narrower than the broad state-of-the-art claim would require, since the comparisons do not include stronger learned rPPG or waveform-reconstruction baselines. In addition, all experiments are conducted on a single dataset. Most importantly, the manuscript defines the record split at the record level but later interprets it as evidence of robustness to unseen individuals; this point needs clarification because the subject-disjointness of that split is not established in the paper as written. One review also appears to overstate the weakness of the empirical gains and to attach unsupported significance language to them; accordingly, I assign limited weight to those aspects of that criticism in the overall assessment.

title: Graph-of-Differences: Anatomy-Structured Difference Alignment for Medical Image Re-identification
reviewer_1_strengths: This is a well-motivated paper on an important problem. In medical image re-identification, retrieval performance alone is not enough; it also matters whether the model’s decision can be related to anatomical structures that a human can inspect. The paper tackles that issue directly by enforcing comparison over named anatomy rather than unconstrained token-space differences. That is a sensible and potentially useful design choice. The technical story is coherent. The anatomy graph construction, soft correspondence, and difference-alignment objective fit together naturally. The ablation study is one of the strongest parts of the paper: simply adding a graph branch is not enough, while correspondence plus alignment produces the main gains. That makes the proposed mechanism more convincing. The explanation analysis is also better than what is often seen in similar papers. Rather than relying only on qualitative saliency maps, the paper includes node insertion/deletion-style faithfulness evaluation with confidence intervals. That gives some evidence that the highlighted nodes are actually used by the model. Finally, the external zero-shot results are encouraging. The fact that gains are still observed on CheXpert and Messidor-2 suggests that the method may be learning somewhat more stable anatomical cues rather than only dataset-specific shortcuts.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: My main concern is the paper’s positioning with respect to prior work. The key claim is that GoD improves on token-space comparison by enforcing anatomical correspondence, but the related-work discussion feels incomplete. In particular, there is a directly relevant prior paper, “Graph Feature Embeddings for Patient Re-Identification from Chest X-Ray Images” (SIBGRAPI 2024), which proposes a graph-based approach for chest X-ray patient re-identification. Even if the proposed formulation here is different, this prior work should be cited and discussed explicitly, since it is close in spirit and problem setting. Without that discussion, the novelty claim feels weaker than it should. A second issue is that the evaluation is somewhat narrow relative to the strength of the claims. The experiments compare mainly against a frozen-backbone baseline and internal ablations. That is a clean design for isolating the effect of the proposed graph-based alignment, and I do appreciate that. However, for a strong methodological paper, I would also want to see comparison against stronger practical baselines, especially end-to-end MedReID systems. This is particularly relevant because the backbone here is MaMI-based, and the original MaMI paper reports stronger results after end-to-end tuning. As written, the paper shows that GoD improves a controlled frozen baseline, but not yet that it is the strongest or most competitive approach overall. The paper’s interpretability claim is promising, but in my view slightly overstated. The node-level explanations are clearly more structured than generic pixel saliency maps, and the insertion/deletion analysis is a meaningful step beyond purely qualitative explanation. Still, “clinically auditable” is a strong claim. The paper does not include clinician studies, expert agreement, or any user-grounded evaluation showing that these explanations actually help humans verify or challenge model decisions. I would therefore frame this more cautiously as improved structure-level interpretability with preliminary faithfulness evidence. Another important limitation is parser dependence. The method relies on modality-specific anatomical parsing to build the graphs, but robustness to noisy or missing masks is not evaluated. Since the practical usefulness of the method depends directly on graph quality, this is not a minor omission. A simple robustness experiment with degraded or partial masks would have strengthened the paper considerably. There are also some presentation issues. The manuscript still contains unresolved cross-references such as “Table ??” and “Tables ??–??,” including in places that matter for the experimental section. This makes the submission feel unfinished. Finally, some of the external improvements, especially on fundus, are fairly small. I would have liked to see confidence intervals or significance testing for those results before drawing a strong conclusion about generalization.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Novel Methodology: The Graph-of-Differences framework introduces a structured way to ground identity comparisons in named anatomical regions rather than arbitrary spatial tokens. This directly addresses shortcut learning, where models rely on scanner artifacts rather than biology. 2.Verifiable Explainability: Unlike unstable pixel-level heatmaps, GoD provides node-level attributions over named structures. The authors quantitatively validate this using node insertion/deletion tests, proving that the attributed nodes are causally linked to the model’s decisions. 3.Strong Empirical Performance: The model demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple modalities. Specifically, it improves Rank-1 by +7.1 pp on fundus and +3.1 pp on CXR over a state-of-the-art frozen-backbone baseline.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Scope Limitations: Currently, the method is limited to 2D images. Extending this to 3D volumetric data (CT/MRI) would require significantly more complex graph correspondence and higher node counts, which the authors acknowledge as future work. 2.Dependency on Parsers: The framework relies heavily on modality-specific anatomical parsers (like CheXmask). Failure or inaccuracies in these masks can degrade the quality of the anatomy graph, which remains a bottleneck for deployment in new modalities. 3.Highly Technical: The paper presents a significant barrier to entry, as the core methodology is difficult to understand without high-level technical knowledge in both graph machine learning and medical imaging.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important issue: lack of interpretability and shortcut learning in medical re-identification. To my perspective, using anatomy to guide comparison is intuitive and meaningful for clinical use. 2.The paper provides a more structured form of explainability by offering node-level explanations tied to specific anatomical regions. This makes the interpretations more meaningful and clinically relevant compared to traditional pixel-based heatmaps, which are often unstable. In addition, the authors include quantitative evaluation through insertion and deletion tests to support the faithfulness of these explanations. 4.The result demonstrates gains across multiple datasets and zero-shot settings and Includes ablation studies and explainability evaluation, supporting the effectiveness of the method.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.There are contents missing in the paper. For example: The experiments section says “All hyperparameters are reported in Table ??” and the explainability section refers to “Fig. 4, Tables ??–??.” There are also potential typo in the paper. For example: ““Interna(ODIR)l”. The author needs to get them fixed. Also, parts of the writing need further polishing to improve readability for a general audience. For example, terms like “R@1” should be clearly defined when first introduced. 2.It lacks detailed information for reproducibility. The paper does not clearly specify batch size, sampling strategy for metric learning, backbone input preprocessing, image resolution, augmentation pipeline, exact identity classification setup, or how external evaluation is done in practice. 3.The paper mainly compares its method to a weaker baseline where the backbone is frozen, plus a few of its own variants. Since GoD is built on top of MaMI, a stronger evaluation would include better baselines, like a fine-tuned MaMI or other existing methods. Right now, the improvements are shown against a limited setup, so it’s unclear how much gain comes from the method itself versus the weaker baseline. 4.The method relies heavily on an anatomy parser, which can be a weakness. If the parser makes mistakes, the graph built from it will also be incorrect, and the model may not work well. In other words, the performance of this method depends on how reliable the parser is. 5.The per-node decomposition {δi} is described as a natural way to audit the model at the node level. However, the paper later states that propagating these attributions to the final embedding z(x) is left for future work, meaning the explanation is not fully complete yet. It needs further explanation. 6.Table 2 reports the backbone-only CXR internal Rank-1 as 0.8659, but Table 3 reports backbone-only CXR Rank-1 as 0.8723 ± 0.0005.Not sure what causes this inconsistency and the author needs to explain it clearly
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers for recognizing GoD’s motivation, the strong ablation (graph alone is inert; correspondence+alignment drive gains), the faithfulness audit, and zero-shot gains. [R2.1] Prior graph-based MedReID. The SIBGRAPI 2024 paper “Graph Feature Embeddings for Patient Re-Identification from Chest X-Ray Images” uses graph features as a single-image embedding; it does not establish per-pair correspondence between named anatomy, compute differences over matched nodes, or provide faithfulness-audited node-level explanations. GoD’s novelty is the per-pair Graph-of-Differences—a structured difference objective enforcing identity comparison over homologous anatomy. We will cite and contrast in Sec.1.[R2.2 / R4.3] Fine-tuned baseline. The frozen backbone in Tab.2 isolated GoD’s contribution from MaMI tuning. We now also report end-to-end fine-tuned MaMI: Method CXR R1 Fundus R1 Backbone frozen : 0.8659 / 0.6396 Backbone fine-tuned (MaMI) : 0.8841 / 0.6712 GoD (frozen backbone) : 0.9033 / 0.7111 GoD (fine-tuned backbone) : 0.9089 / 0.7253 GoD’s gain is orthogonal to backbone tuning: on fine-tuned MaMI it still adds +2.5 pp CXR/+5.4 pp fundus, and the best absolute result is GoD+fine-tuned. [R2.3] Interpretability framing. We agree “clinically auditable” overstates current evidence. We will revise throughout to “structure-level interpretability with quantitative faithfulness evidence”—what insertion/deletion tests show — and note full auditability requires radiologist user studies (future work). [R2.4/R3.2/R4.4/R5.2] Parser robustness. Soft correspondence (Eq.5) absorbs parser errors via row-softmax down-weighting mismatched/missing nodes. Stress test (CXR R1/Fundus R1): Perturbation CXR Fundus Clean (default) : 0.9033 / 0.7111 10% nodes dropped randomly : 0.8987 / 0.7044 30% nodes dropped : 0.8821 / 0.6852 50% nodes dropped : 0.8543 / 0.6517 5-px mask dilation : 0.8951 / 0.7038 10-px mask dilation : 0.8782 / 0.6859 No graph (frozen backbone) : 0.8659 / 0.6396 GoD stays above the no-graph baseline through 50% node dropout and 10-px mask noise. Added to Sec-4.[R2.5/R4.1] Presentation. We will fix unresolved cross-references (Table??), the “Interna(ODIR)l” typo, and define R@1 at first use. [R2.6] External CIs. Messidor-2 external gain will carry bootstrap 95% CIs: GoD R1 = 0.6579 [0.6491,0.6664] vs. backbone 0.6499 [0.6398,0.6604]. [R4.2] Reproducibility. We will add: batch 64, BatchHard sampler, 224x224 input, ImageNet normalization, label smoothing 0.1, plus the external-eval protocol. [R4.5] Per-node attribution propagation. Per-node delta_i are read from the graph branch where the alignment loss directly operates, so the insertion/deletion audit targets exactly the component the attributions describe—tight by construction. Propagating through the fused embedding z(x) requires learned credit assignment, which we defer rather than approximate: an approximate propagation would conflate graph-branch faithfulness with fusion gating and weaken the current guarantee. [R4.6] Tab.2/Tab.3 inconsistency. 0.8659 (Tab.2) is a single seed; 0.8723+-0.0005 (Tab.3) is the three-seed mean. We will report the seed-averaged value in both. [R3.1/R5.3] 3D extension. GoD transfers directly to 3D: replace 2D parsers with volumetric segmentors (TotalSegmentator) and the node encoder with a coord-aware GNN for denser graphs and 3D correspondence. We list this as immediate future work. [R3.3] Accessibility. We will add a short intuition paragraph in Sec.2 introducing the graph-of-differences idea before the formal definitions. [R5.1/R5.4] Reader study and explanation depth. Insertion/deletion tests establish faithfulness; clinician studies establish utility. A forced-choice reader study with collaborating clinicians (GoD node-level vs. pixel-saliency baselines on agreement and verification time) planned in post-camera-ready.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: N/A Justification(s): This is promising and well-motivated work with a strong empirical element. All reviewers agree that the work addresses an important limitation in MedReID and appreciate the explainability contribution and relatively comprehensive experimental validation. However, some concerns remain regarding dependence on parsers, robustness, baseline comparisons and interpretability claims. There are also some minor presentation issues to rectify. If results exist, the fine-tuned model should be reported; otherwise, the authors must justify the frozen backbone. The authors should also demonstrate some evidence of robustness of the parser and review the claims of interpretability. It is also important to clarify the distinction from existing work. | N/A Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes a graph-based framework for anatomy-based re-identification, R3 and R5 liked the explainability approach. R2 and R4 has concerns on missing fine-tuned baselines, reproducibility details, and dependence on parser. R2 and R4 did not provide feedback on rebuttal. The rebuttal addressed most of the concerns (showing orthogonal performance from requested baselines). For all these reasons, and with respect to the other submissions, the recommendation is towards Acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal directly addresses the key concerns by adding fine-tuned MaMI results, parser-robustness stress tests, external confidence intervals, reproducibility details, a clearer distinction from prior graph-based MedReID work, and a more cautious interpretability framing; therefore, despite remaining limitations on clinician validation and 3D extension, I support acceptance.

title: MBFAD: Benchmarking Balance Function Assessment with Environmental Perturbation and Synergistic Tasks
reviewer_1_strengths: MBFAD combines whole-body kinematics, plantar pressure, reactive tasks, and perturbation-based acquisition in a single dataset. Table 1 compares MBFAD with prior datasets and shows that MBFAD uniquely includes kinematics, pressure, reactive activities, and perturbation together. The acquisition setup is also clearly illustrated in Figure 1. Using activity recognition as a prior for balance assessment is sensible because stability risk is context-dependent across activities. The paper explicitly formulates this distinction in Section 3.1.It operationalizes it through parallel HAR and BFA streams in Section 3.2, along with an architecture diagram, making the design easy to follow (although some details are missing). The comparison against multiple baselines on SisFall and PDS includes modality and task ablations on MBFAD in Tables 2 to 4.This is good experimental practice and strengthens the argument that both multimodality and joint learning matter.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The most substantial contribution to the field is the MBFAD, which contains 29 subjects, all young adults around 20 to 22 years old. The motivation of the paper is about fall prevention and balance health. The absence of older adults or clinical populations is a serious limitation for translational claims. The data may still be useful as a technical benchmark, but the current cohort is not representative of the target populations most at risk. The paper presents only in Figure 2, the necessary data preprocessing steps (coordinate alignment, timestamp, sliding window, etc). None of these steps is explicitly presented. The details needed to reproduce the results are not provided, so the explanation of data collection and processing is limited. Also, no description of the training and inference details (optimizer, epochs, learning rate, etc. ). There are no details in the data or the splits (are they the same as in [22]?) It is not clearly explained how the balance function labels, especially the high/ low risk labels, were assigned. The authors mentioned that, with two rehabilitation experts and without a precise label-generation protocol, it is difficult to fully assess whether the labels are strong enough to support future clinical claims. The conclusion discusses the broader implications of moving toward context-aware stability analysis and suggests future value in this direction. However, the paper does not address key limitations, including a young, small cohort, a lack of clinical validation, and insufficient evidence for generalization to real patient populations.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper presents several notable strengths. First, it introduces a novel multimodal benchmark (MBFAD) for balance and fall assessment that explicitly models static, dynamic, and reactive activity paradigms, which is more comprehensive than many existing datasets. Second, the incorporation of sensory perturbation via an air cushion is an original idea that enables controlled simulation of balance disturbances, providing a more realistic experimental setup compared to standard recordings. Third, the proposed M²-Balance Framework leverages a shared encoder for jointly learning human activity recognition (HAR) and balance/fall assessment (BFA), which is a meaningful multitask formulation that can improve representation learning. Finally, the authors validate their approach on both the collected dataset and public benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements over baseline methods, which supports the generalizability of the approach.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper has several important weaknesses. First, the evaluation protocol is insufficiently described and potentially flawed, as it is unclear whether subject-independent validation (e.g., leave-one-subject-out or subject-wise splits) is used, raising concerns about possible data leakage. Second, the reported results appear to rely mainly on sliding window-level metrics, without providing sequence-, trial-, or subject-level evaluation, which limits practical relevance. Third, although the paper reports p-values, the statistical analysis is not properly described. The authors do not specify which statistical tests were used, whether assumptions were checked, or how multiple comparisons were handled, making it difficult to assess the validity of the claimed significance. Finally, the clinical applicability is limited, as the dataset appears to be collected primarily from younger adults, while fall risk assessment is most relevant for geriatric populations. The lack of validation on elderly or clinical cohorts reduces the translational impact of the work.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The newly acquired dataset MBFAD that consists of data of 29 subjects for 14 activities, using 16 IMU sensors on the body and 32 in-sole sensors for each shoe, is a good contribution. In addition, authors also implement and evaluate a new AI model, called M^2-balance for (presumably) 14-class classification for activity recognition, and binary classification for balance function assessment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: This reviewer has the following comments: Consider additional age groups, of middle age people and possibly elderly Authors may want to define/describe all 14 activities done by each of the 29 subjects, under berg or brunel scale methods. They should especially explain the sensory perturbation-based motions and reactive motion. In section I, authors state that they have collected kinematics data from 59 body locations, while in section II, they state that they have used 16 9-axis IMU sensors for kinematics data collection. Is each IMU sensor at a given location measuring more than one body organ/element? Please reconcile both statements. The variables L, H,W,C represent the dimensions of the feature maps, but are not defined in Eqs. 1,2.- In section 3.3, authors make mention of G groups? Is G=14, corresponding to 14 different activities that subjects do? Or, does it mean something else? Authors may want to explain the rationale/reasoning behind Eq. 2.In order words, why did they decide to split the intermediate feature map into two maps and then to concatenate the first half O_1^1 with the next group F^{i+1}? Is F^i from Eq. 2 and F_n from Eq. 3 the same? If so, then better to use a consistent notation. Or, are they different? What is N in Eq. 3? What is the motivation for Eq. 3 that shows us the absolute difference of two convolutions (of the feature map with the kernel), that is then averaged over N? Eq. 6: Authors may want to do an ablation on parameters alpha and beta, to learn more about their individual contributions. Also, authors may want to define the two loss functions. Overall, the mathematical description of the proposed AI model (M^2-balance) needs improvement in terms of rigor. Authors seem to have fully omitted the key data pre-processing details which is something very important to better understand the contribution of this work, and for the reproducibility of this work. They show a glimpse of their pre-processing pipeline in Fig. 2, but do not talk about it in the paper at all. Similarly, authors make mention of the 2 feature extractors MotionNet and PressureNet in Fig. 2, but again, they don’t mention important details such as backbone architecture of these 2 encoders in the paper at all. Authors present their results in results section, but without specifying the precise details of the problem being solved. That is, for activity recognition problem, they probably have solved a 14-class classification problem (as hinted in Fig. 2). If that is the case, they need to mention it in the results section (Table 2) with clarity. Table 2: Authors do not describe their data splitting methodology, and of the related works. Thus, it is not possible to infer something meaningful out of these results unless and until we get to know the data splitting methodology for all the works (related works, and authors’ work). And as authors may already know, the leave some subjects out cross validation methodology is the preferred data splitting method, as otherwise there will be data leakage between train and test sets. For the BFA task, authors report the results in table 3, 4.However, I would like to know how authors have computed the accuracy values for this task. I mean, Fig. 2 tells me that authors solve a binary classification problem here (low risk, high risk). How do authors compute the fall risk to be high or low, for a given subject? I would also like to know the data splitting methodology for this task as well. What is the fate of the collected MBFAD dataset? Will it be made public for the benefit of fellow researchers? Overall, the paper presents an interesting idea, i.e., a new MBFAD dataset and M^2-balance AI model. However, there is an ambiguity regarding the results reported in the results section, because authors have not mentioned the data splitting methodology, as well as the key data pre-processing details. Also, the mathematical explanation of proposed M^2-balance framework requires polishing and improvement. Finally, it is not clear whether authors plan to release their collected dataset to the public.

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): I recommend an Accept based on the consensus of the reviewers, who all provided positive evaluations. The reviewers unanimously praised the introduction of the MBFAD benchmark, noting its novel integration of synchronized whole-body kinematics, plantar pressure, and reactive activities, along with the original use of sensory perturbation via an air cushion to simulate authentic balance disturbances. Furthermore, the proposed M²-Balance framework was commended for its synergistic, multi-task approach that jointly learns human activity recognition and balance assessment to improve representation learning. While the core contributions are strong, the reviewers raised several methodological and clinical points that must be addressed in the camera-ready version. The authors must clarify the evaluation protocol, specifically detailing whether subject-independent data splitting was employed to prevent data leakage between the training and testing sets. They also need to enhance reproducibility by including thorough descriptions of the data preprocessing steps, training hyperparameters, and the specific backbone architectures of the feature extractors. Additionally, the mathematical descriptions require refinement to explicitly define all variables, such as L, H, W, C, G, and N , and clearly explain the rationale behind the feature map splitting and the joint loss function parameters. From a clinical perspective, the authors must acknowledge the dataset’s limitation of comprising primarily young adults and discuss the generalizability and translational applicability of these results to older, at-risk geriatric cohorts. Finally, the manuscript must explicitly clarify the protocol used by the rehabilitation experts to assign the high-risk and low-risk balance function labels and detail the specific statistical tests utilized to compute the reported p-values. Addressing these clarifications will significantly strengthen the final manuscript.

title: mSpecFusion-Net: Intelligent Multimodal Smartphone Imaging for Mobile Differential Diagnosis of Psoriasis and Dermatitis and Deep Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Innovative Hardware-Software Integration: The combination of an 8-band LED multiplexer with polarization filters and UV autofluorescence on a mobile device seems highly innovative. It provides a unique solution to the limitations of standard RGB imaging. 2.Rigorous Validation Strategy: The use of patient-wise 5-fold cross-validation is excellent. In dermatology AI, random splitting often leads to severe data leakage (where the model learns the patient’s background skin rather than the disease). The authors correctly avoided this pitfall. 3.Strong Ablation Studies: The paper does an excellent job of justifying its complexity. Table 2 proves the utility of PCA, Table 3 validates the iterative fusion module over standard early/late fusion (even though there are concerns regarding this table), and Table 4 confirms the necessity of the multimodal hardware setup. 4.Clinical Relevance: Targeting Psoriasis vs. Seborrheic Dermatitis is a highly practical objective, as these are notoriously difficult to distinguish in primary care and RGB teledermatology. 5.Architectural Innovation: The use of PCA, the concept of iterative fusion, and the overall design seem sufficiently novel and well motivated.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The major weakness of this paper is the lack of clarity and incompleteness when it comes to the evaluations against SOTA architectures and fusion methods. I am listing them below: 1.Ambiguity in Evaluation Metrics (Patch vs. Patient Level): Section 2.4 states that images are “partitioned into a fixed grid of nonoverlapping patches” and that these patches are used as training instances. However, the evaluation tables (Tables 2-5) do not clarify if the reported F1, Accuracy, and AUC metrics are evaluated at the patch-level, image-level, or patient-level. Why this matters: If a model predicts 100 patches from a single patient’s image and gets 90 right, patch-level metrics will look fantastic, but clinically, we only care about the single image/patient diagnosis. The authors must report patient-level or image-level aggregated metrics (e. g. , via majority voting across patches). 2.Missing PCA Parameters: The paper mentions applying PCA to the multispectral stacks to reduce inter-wavelength redundancy, but omits critical reproducibility details. How many principal components were retained? What percentage of variance was explained by the retained components? 3.Unfair Baseline Comparisons: In Table 5, the proposed model is compared to standard backbones. It is unclear how these baselines processed the multimodal data. Did they receive a concatenated tensor of all modalities (early fusion)? If these baselines were only given RGB images, or if they were not adapted to handle the high-dimensional multispectral stacks properly, the comparison to mSpecFusion-Net is an apples-to-oranges comparison. It doesn’t add any value at all. How these baselines were attained needs critical attention. 4.Fusion Methods: Similarly, Table 3 mentions fusion methods, but fails to provide any detail whatsoever on the specifics (late fusion, how? Concatenation? Attention? Gated?) 5.Lack of comparison to recent works: The authors fail to compare their work against recent multimodal, multispectral, and fusion-based studies. For example, the following papers could be discussed to outline the improvements: i) https://doi. org/10.1016/j. ibmed. 2025.100271 ii) https://doi. org/10.1109/JBHI. 2026.3682634
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis often present with similar visual appearances, making research on mobile screening and remote dermatological diagnosis highly clinically relevant. This paper proposes a coherent end-to-end framework that includes a smartphone-based multimodal dermoscope, acquisition and calibration procedures, and a dedicated multimodal analysis model. As a result, its contribution is more practically meaningful than that of a purely retrospective classification study. The proposed iterative fusion design is a meaningful innovation. It allows the model to progressively exchange and refine cross-modal evidence. The results suggest that this strategy outperforms conventional fusion approaches. The full multimodal iterative fusion model performs clearly better than the RGB-only input setting, demonstrating that explicitly modeling multimodal complementarity is more effective than simply extending generic architectures.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The method used in this paper integrates parallel modality encoders, Transformer-based fusion, PCA-based spectral compression, and iterative multimodal fusion. While the use of these components is reasonable, the work does not demonstrate a strongly novel algorithmic advance. In my view, the most distinctive contribution of this paper lies in the multimodal mobile diagnostic workflow rather than in a fundamentally new core algorithmic design. During training, the authors divide the images into non-overlapping patches and assign patient-level diagnostic labels to each patch. I am concerned that this strategy may reduce lesion-level contextual information and may not fully reflect how dermatologists integrate the overall morphology of a lesion in clinical practice. I would encourage the authors to provide more discussion to justify this design choice. Given that the goal of this work is mobile-device-based diagnosis, the paper should report more information on acquisition time, inference time, computational cost, and operational complexity. I encourage the authors to more fully quantify the practical burden of the entire multimodal workflow in order to demonstrate the deployability of the proposed framework. The presentation of symbols and formulas in the manuscript is not sufficiently clear. For example, the meaning of F in Figure 1 is not explained in the text. I encourage the authors to improve these aspects to enhance the overall quality of the manuscript.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: – Paper is well written. Motivation is well presented. – The proposed mSpecFusion-Net architecture, using iterative fusion, seems to be a novel approach for integrating complementary information across modalities. The results presented indicate that this improves the robustness compared to simpler fusion methods – Considering 5-fold cross validation in experiments for comparative analysis – Considering and addressing the issue of inter-wavelength redundancy using PCA for improved performance
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Limited novelty as there has been Smartphone-based multispectral imaging systems (mentioned by authors as well). Comparison with traditional 2019-2021 DL methods only (ResNet, ViT, efficientNet, etc) No discussion of statistical significance results and standard deviation of 5-fold cross validation. No computational complexity related discussion Reproducibility concerns. No discussion by authors regarding providing codes and dataset, or making these available later. Differences with paper [6] not clearly highlighted. Following related paper not considered (Wang et al., “Enhancing Diagnosis of Psoriasis and Inflammatory Skin Diseases: A Spatially Aligned Multimodal Model Integrating Clinical and Dermoscopic Images”, Journal of Investigative Dermatology, Volume 145, Issue 11, November 2025)
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers and the meta-reviewer. We address the main concerns below; minor points will be addressed in the camera-ready revision. Evaluation and cross-validation (R1, R2, Meta). All metrics in Tables 2–5 are at the patch level under strict patient-wise 5-fold CV: 32 patients are split into 10 disjoint patient-level groups; per round, 2 groups (~20%) form the test set, 1 validation, 7 training. The test partitions are disjoint and cover all patients, so each appears in exactly one test set, with no identity leakage. Patch predictions can be aggregated by averaging or voting at the lesion/patient level for deployment. PCA (R1, Meta). PCA is used as discrete band selection on calibrated multispectral stacks, not as a learned feature projection. We rank the 8 bands by cumulative absolute PCA loading and retain the top K=4 per polarization stream. Since this is discrete index selection rather than data-dependent transformation, it is performed once on the calibrated dataset and fixed across folds; parameter learning remains strictly fold-independent, so the leakage pattern typically associated with global preprocessing does not apply. Statistical reporting (R3). Across 5 folds, the model achieves F1 = 0.9057 ± 0.0612, Acc = 0.9068 ± 0.0576, ROC-AUC = 0.9461 ± 0.0540, PRC-AUC = 0.9358 ± 0.0666 (mean ± SD, micro). One fold yields F1 = 0.8174, reflecting the modest cohort; larger multi-site validation is future work. Computational cost (R3, Meta). Acquisition takes ~20 s/patient. The model has 4.18 M parameters (16.0 MB, fp32) and 44.7 GFLOPs/image (bs=1), with GPU latency 17.3 ms/image (median, 100 runs). Inference is negligible vs. acquisition, so point-of-care latency is dominated by acquisition. Ethics (R3). The study was approved by the IRB of Seoul National University Hospital (No. 1908-161-1059), with informed consent from all participants. We will add this to the clinical dataset section. Baseline fairness (R1). All baselines in Table 5 receive the same multimodal input (Co-P + Cross-P MSI with PCA + UV-AF) under the same split and protocol; RGB-only is in Table 4.We will clarify this in the Table 5 caption. Comparison with related work (R1, R2). Yang et al. and Siddiqui et al. (S3F-Net) maximize information from single-modality images via anatomical metadata and Fourier features. Our work fuses modalities from distinct physical principles, requires no metadata, and enables acquisition by non-specialists. Wang et al. uses dermoscopic and clinical images, both RGB; our multi-physical-modality approach is fundamentally different. We will add this to the Introduction. Use of recent baselines (R1, R2). We additionally tested ConvNeXt V2-Base and ConvNeXt V2-Large using the same training protocol and input setting. Both models underperformed our proposed method: ConvNeXt V2-Base achieved an F1 score of 0.736 ± 0.187, and ConvNeXt V2-Large achieved 0.567 ± 0.171, whereas our method achieved 0.906 ± 0.061.Moreover, their per-fold standard deviations (~0.17–0.19) were approximately three times higher than that of our method (0.061). Novelty (R1, R2). The key contribution is the development of an intelligent mobile multimodal framework for robust smartphone-based skin lesion assessment. Rather than relying on simple multimodal concatenation, conventional early/late fusion, or generic backbone scaling, our framework combines PCA-based spectral compression with iterative cross-modal fusion to progressively refine complementary optical evidence from co-polarized, cross-polarized, multispectral reflectance, and UV autofluorescence modalities. This model-level integration enables compact spectral representation, effective use of modality-specific and cross-modal cues, and more stable learning in a modest-sized clinical cohort. Code will be released upon publication. Typos and notation (R3). We will correct typos (e.g., “deelp learing”), clarify notation, and refine the technical descriptions throughout.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): Given the overall positive reviews, I recommend acceptance. Please address the following concerns in the final version: (1) clarify evaluation protocols, particularly whether metrics are reported at patch-, image-, or patient-level; (2) include missing methodological details; and (3) discuss practical deployment aspects such as computational cost and workflow feasibility. Addressing these points will be important to confirm the strength of the contribution.

title: Propagating Structural Guidance: Synthesizing Fluorescein Angiography from Fundus Images and Sparse OCT Scans
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The idea of synthesizing FFA from CFP with OCT guidance is clinically meaningful, since both OCT and CFP are non-invasive modalities and therefore more feasible in real-world practice. 2.Incorporating OCT as an auxiliary modality provides additional structural supervision, which plausibly contributes to the improved synthesis performance. 3.The proposed method is designed with clinical considerations in mind, and the downstream experiments provide further evidence of its effectiveness and potential utility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to a single dataset, making it difficult to assess the robustness and generalizability of the proposed method across different clinical centers, populations, and imaging devices.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novelty of Dataset: The authors propose a novel method by incorporating OCT into CFP-to-FFA synthesis and construct a large-scale, paired tri-modal retinal dataset, which fills a significant gap in the field. Methodological Soundness: The Trajectory-Aware En-face Projection is effectively designed by accounting for the inherent acquisition differences between OCT and CFP. Comprehensive Experimental Design: The evaluation extends beyond standard visual fidelity. By validating the synthesized FFAs in downstream classification tasks, the authors demonstrate the practical utility of the generated images. Furthermore, the inclusion of a discussion on the ratio of OCT during training provides convincing evidence for the effectiveness of OCT guidance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Limited Comparison to State-of-the-Art: While the authors cite relevant works such as “ Lesion-aware generative adversarial networks for color fundus image to fundus fluorescein angiography translation” and “ Non-invasive to invasive: Enhancing FFA synthesis from CFP with a benchmark dataset and a novel network”, a quantitative comparison against these specific baseline methods is absent. Lack of Statistical Rigor: There is no statistical evaluation for the classification performance; the absence of standard deviations makes it difficult to assess the stability and reliability of the reported improvements. Lack of Sensitivity Analysis: The experimental section is missing a parameter sensitivity analysis, particularly regarding the hyper-parameter β in the loss function. It remains unclear how different weights affect the synthesis performance. Insufficient Discussion on Limitations: The qualitative analysis focuses exclusively on successful cases. The paper would benefit from a dedicated section on failure cases and a discussion of the model’s boundary conditions. Lack of Visionary Discussion: There is limited discussion on the distinct clinical roles of CFP, FFA, and OCT. For CFP-to-FFA synthesis to be truly impactful, the authors should discuss whether synthesized FFAs can genuinely substitute for real FFAs in clinical workflows. Incorporating human expert evaluation (e.g., a Turing test by ophthalmologists) would significantly strengthen the argument for its practical application.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Strong novelty: The work is the first to use OCT as structural guidance for FFA synthesis. This is clinically well-motivated since OCT is non-invasive and available in scenarios where FFA is contraindicated. 2.Dataset contribution: The tri-modal dataset (3,676 cases with registration pipeline) is a genuine and valuable contribution to the community, especially given the scarcity of paired multi-modal retinal datasets. 3.Well-designed SACMF: The trajectory-aware projection is an elegant solution to the OCT–fundus viewpoint discrepancy. Propagating structural cues via CFP-based attention to unscanned regions is practical and effective. 4.Comprehensive evaluation: Both standard image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, FID, LPIPS) and downstream diagnostic utility (disease classification) are evaluated. The code is publicly available. 5.Clinically meaningful upper/lower bound analysis provides context for interpreting results.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited dataset size and split: With only 3,676 cases and a 60/40 train/test split, the dataset is relatively small for a generative model. The choice of 40% for testing is unusual and reduces training data; the rationale should be discussed. 2.GAN instability not discussed: The paper adopts a GAN backbone without discussing training stability, mode coverage, or failure cases. Given the small dataset, GAN training risks are non-trivial. 3.OCT sparsity assumption: The method assumes sparse B-scans are available alongside CFP. This may not always hold in clinical practice. The sensitivity to number and placement of OCT scans is only partially explored (20%-100% training ratio, but not inference-time availability). 4.Qualitative results are limited: Only 4 rows of examples are shown in Figure 2.More diverse failure cases or challenging pathologies would strengthen the qualitative analysis. 5.TCMA supervision detail: It is not fully clear how the FFA tokens are obtained during inference (when real FFA is unavailable), suggesting TCMA may only be active during training.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Dataset Size and Split Constrain Generalization Thank you for your valuable feedback. Compared to large-scale datasets in natural image domains, the cost of data acquisition in medical image generation tasks is relatively high, and thus data scale remains an important challenge in this field. However, it is worth noting that in the specific task of fundus image to FFA synthesis, the data scales used in existing publicly available studies are generally small. For example: “Diabetic retinopathy grading by digital curvelet transform” includes only 59 cases, covering only normal and diabetic retinopathy. “Lesion-aware generative adversarial networks for color fundus image to fundus fluorescein angiography translation” includes 133 cases, with only BRVO. “Non-Invasive to Invasive: Enhancing FFA Synthesis from CFP with a Benchmark Dataset and a Novel Network” includes 600 cases, covering five disease categories. In comparison, our dataset contains 3,676 cases, with 8 disease categories having more than 100 cases each. Under this task setting, our dataset is significantly larger than existing works and covers a richer distribution of lesions. Regarding the data split ratio, we adopted a 60/40 train/test split rather than the more common 80/20 or 70/30, primarily to enlarge the test set size, thereby enabling a more reliable evaluation of the model’s generalization ability. Therefore, we aim to more thoroughly evaluate the model’s performance on unseen cases, different lesion types, and varying severity levels through a larger test set. Additionally, it should be noted that compared to the data scales of 59, 133, or 600 cases in existing works, our dataset contains 3,676 cases. Even with a 60/40 split, the training set size remains significantly larger than those used in existing methods. 2.Clarification on TCMA Supervision and Inference Thank you for pointing this out. TCMA is used only during training as an auxiliary supervision module, leveraging ground-truth FFA tokens to provide cross-modal constraints. During inference, the model takes only CFP as input and does not require FFA tokens. We have clarified this distinction in the revised manuscript 3.Insufficient Discussion on Limitations and Failure Cases Thank you for this suggestion. We have added failure case analysis and a discussion of model limitations in the Qualitative Comparison section of the revised manuscript. Meanwhile, we have illustrated a representative failure case in Fig. 2(b) to provide a clear visual example. In this discussion, we explicitly acknowledge certain limitations of our model: (1) vessel boundaries may appear blurred, and (2) the model struggles to recover very small or widely distributed leakage regions, resulting in incomplete synthesis. 4.Undiscussed GAN Training Instability First, with proper architectural design and training techniques, the training stability of GAN frameworks is no longer a major issue. Our GAN model exhibits stable training behavior without evident failure phenomena such as mode collapse. Second, we have also carefully considered and experimented with Diffusion-based methods. As shown in Table 1, we implemented BBDM as a comparative method, but its performance was notably inferior to the GAN-based version. We further attempted to improve its performance by increasing the number of training epochs, yet the gains were not significant. We attribute this primarily to the fact that, in the absence of a large-scale pretrained VAE, directly modeling in pixel-level space poses greater challenges for Diffusion methods, whereas GANs demonstrate better adaptability and stability in such medical image cross-modal generation tasks.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a clinically meaningful multimodal framework for synthesizing FFA from CFP with structural guidance from OCT. Reviewers agree that the problem is highly relevant, and the approach is novel, particularly through the integration of OCT guidance and the construction of a tri-modal dataset. The method is well-designed and supported by a comprehensive evaluation, including downstream clinical tasks. The concerns are mostly about strengthening the experimental analysis and clarifications rather than fundamental flaws.

title: PROTON: Prototype-Based Test-Time Online OOD Detection for Medical VLMs
reviewer_1_strengths: Strengths: The paper is well-written and the identified problem (\i. e. , detecting both semantic-shift and covariate-shift) is interesting to the community. Extensive experiments have been done to valid the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Weaknesses: It is true the the proposed framework is free from accessing the training data, however, it necessities to access test samples. Meanwhile, the construction of the prototype bank initially relies on the reliability of confidence score (\i. e. , MCM), however, one of motivations of this work is that MCM is unreliable to detect the covariate-shift OOD samples. Imagine that if the beginning sampels are mostly covariate-shift OOD samples, then the quality of prototype bank might be degraded. I believe the authors miss one important work TAG [1], which does not rely on the model modification, training data, and prompt engineering. The authors are encouraged to incorporate the results of OOD detection using TAG as one of baselines. [1] TAG: Text Prompt Augmentation for Zero-Shot Out-of-Distribution Detection, ECCV, 2024.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The proposed online prototype bank does not require access to training data, which is particularly valuable in medical applications where data privacy and restricted data sharing are major practical concerns. 2.The method shows clear empirical gains over strong baseline methods, with especially significant improvements on covariate shift while also consistently improving semantic and far-OOD detection. 3.The ablation and sensitivity studies suggest that the method is robust to hyperparameter choices, which strengthens its practicality for real deployment settings.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.A limitation of the paper is that the method is mainly validated on top of MCM. The authors claim that PROTON is compatible with other scoring functions, but they do not provide enough empirical evidence to show that it can reliably improve non-MCM scores as well. 2.The empirical comparison is not sufficiently broad. In particular, only a small number of non-MCM-style baselines are considered, and these are relatively old methods, which weakens the strength of the experimental validation. 3.The method strongly depends on high classification accuracy of the base model. If the model makes incorrect predictions, the prototype bank can be contaminated and may even fail completely. However, the paper does not discuss this sensitivity or analyze performance when the classifier is weak.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: I think the paper identifies a clear and well-characterized failure mode. The observation that covariate-shifted inputs are indistinguishable in softmax space but separable in embedding space (Figure 1) is compelling. The t-SNE plots, MCM score overlap analysis, and 2D scatter of MCM vs. prototype distance all provide direct evidence, which I find convincing. This is not just a hand-wavy motivation. The method design is also elegant. PROTON adds no learnable parameters, requires a single forward pass, and uses O(1) memory per update via Welford’s algorithm. The confidence gate to prevent OOD contamination of prototypes is a small but important detail. I think the idea of using MCM variance to automatically detect when softmax confidence becomes unreliable (Eq. 3-4) is clever. The sigmoid interpolation avoids hard switching, and the behavior analysis showing αt dropping when covariate samples enter demonstrates the mechanism works as intended. When I look at the ablation (Table 2), I appreciate that it systematically decomposes contributions: prototype distance (+15.5 covariate AUROC), adaptive fusion (+4.8), and confidence gate (+3.6). The γ × M sensitivity analysis across three medical domains (Figure 3b) also shows the method is robust across a wide range of hyperparameters, which is reassuring for practical deployment.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: My main concern is that the full evaluation is conducted on a single benchmark (FLAIR + FIVES) for the main results. The ID set contains only 300 samples (150 Normal + 150 DR) and OOD sets are similarly small. For a method that relies on online prototype accumulation, the stream length matters. The γ × M heatmaps in Figure 3b show results on radiology and pathology, but only as ∆AUROC without absolute numbers or dataset details. I would have liked to see full Table 1-style results on at least one additional domain. Also, the method assumes the test stream contains a sufficient proportion of in-distribution samples to build meaningful prototypes. In deployment scenarios where most incoming samples are OOD (e.g., a screening system receiving many misrouted images), the prototype bank could be contaminated despite the confidence gate. The paper does not analyze sensitivity to the ID/OOD ratio in the stream, and I am curious about how the method degrades in such scenarios. Another point I think is that hierarchical MCM (L=5) achieves 87.7% covariate AUROC versus PROTON’s 66.3%, which is a gap of over 20 points. While the authors note this requires domain-expert prompt trees, the performance difference is substantial and I think should be discussed more openly. The prototype convergence analysis (Figure 3a) is also shown only for radiology and pathology, not for the primary ophthalmology benchmark, which is an odd choice.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers for recognizing PROTON’s novelty, motivation, and clean ablations. We address all the comments below. [R2.1] Beyond MCM. PROTON needs only a scalar base score S_b and embedding e_t: S_PROTON^b = a_t S_b_hat + (1-a_t) S_proto_hat; MCM is one instantiation. Across six base scores, PROTON improves every one on all shifts (mean +11-15 AUROC). Cov AUROC (base->+PROTON): MaxLogit 42.8->62.5; GL-MCM 43.5->65.8; Energy 43.8->62.0; MCM 42.4->66.3; Entropy 44.1->63.1; TAG-MCM 45.7->67.1.Semantic and far-OOD follow the same pattern. The contribution is image-embedding geometry — a complement to any softmax/logit score, not an MCM trick. [R2.2] Broader baselines. We add TAG-MCM (ECCV’24), Hier.MCM(L=5), and privileged ID-feature banks. Cov AUROC: TAG-MCM 45.7; kNN-ID 70.8, Mahalanobis-ID 68.6 (labeled ID features); Hier.MCM(L=5) 87.7 (LLM prompts); PROTON 66.3 (no train, no prompts); Hier.MCM+PROTON 88.4.PROTON matches privileged feature-bank methods without training data or prompts, and composes with Hier.MCM. [R2.3] Sensitivity to classifier accuracy. Under forced misrouting, PROTON stays above MCM through 30% misrouting (65.5 vs 57.6 mean). The confidence gate (g=0.7) alone adds +3.6 cov-AUROC (Tab.2) by blocking OOD contamination; pure-MCM fallback (Alg.1) holds before K_min. We will add a conservative gate (confidence+margin+prototype-consistency) with base-score fallback when unstable. [R1.1] Cold-start and online setting. PROTON is strictly online: x_t is scored using the bank from past accepted samples; the bank updates only after (B_t = Update(B_{t-1}, e_t) iff max_c p_{t,c} >= g). No labels, transduction, or model updates. Before all classes reach K_min, PROTON falls back to pure MCM (Alg. 1). The score is a fusion S_PROTON = a_t S_MCM + (1-a_t) S_proto — MCM only gates which samples enter the bank; the OOD decision uses S_proto, capturing the embedding separation MCM misses. Stream ID-fraction (Sem/Cov/Far AUROC): rho=90%: 63.2/67.4/84.8; rho=70%: 62.7/66.3/84.5 (default) rho=30%: 58.8/58.5/80.4; rho=10%: 55.1/50.9/77.2; MCM: 53.9/42.4/76.4 PROTON stays above MCM down to 10% ID. Stream-order CIs (5 perms): 62.7+-1.1 / 66.3+-1.8 / 84.5+-0.9 (order-stable). The non-zero ID-fraction assumption will be stated explicitly. [R1.2] TAG baseline. Added — see [R2.2]. TAG-MCM (45.7 cov-AUROC) underperforms PROTON (66.3) and is orthogonal: TAG augments text prompts, PROTON exploits image-embedding geometry. Using TAG-MCM as PROTON’s base score yields 67.1. [R3.1] Cross-domain / cross-VLM. We replace dAUROC heatmaps with absolute Table 1-style numbers across three VLMs/domains. Cov AUROC (MCM->PROTON): Ophth. (FLAIR) 42.4->66.3; Radio. (UniMedCLIP) 44.7->90.4; Patho. (QuiltNet) 45.3->84.2.Gains are largest on covariate shift; semantic and far-OOD also improve everywhere (full metrics in appendix). Datasets: Radio. = Normal/Pneumonia (RSNA, 300 ea.); Patho. = Benign/Malignant (PCam-derived, 300 ea.). [R3.2] ID/OOD stream-ratio. See [R1.1]- PROTON stays above MCM down to 10% ID. In low-ID screening, the confidence gate+K_min fallback keep prototypes uncontaminated; pure-MCM is recovered in the worst case, so PROTON never degrades below baseline. [R3.3] Hier.MCM gap and FLAIR convergence. The 21-point cov-AUROC gap is real: Hier.MCM uses LLM-generated prompt trees, PROTON uses none. They are complementary — Hier.MCM+PROTON reaches 88.4 cov-AUROC, and PROTON exceeds Hier.MCM on far-OOD (84.5 vs 82.4). PROTON’s distinct value: zero training data, prompt trees, or expert input. The FLAIR convergence plot will be added (cos to final prototype >0.99 within ~55 samples; parallels Fig.3a). [R3.4] sigma_0^2 and shift-type triage. sigma_0^2 is not tuned per-VLM: sweeping {0.005-0.08} gives flat mean AUROC 69.8-71.2 (sigmoid saturation). 0.02 corresponds to early-stream ID variance from a brief warm-up. The (S_MCM, S_proto) decomposition supports shift-type triage with macro-F1 = 0.70 on 3-way Cov/Sem/Far classification.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: ActiveX VT_ERROR: Post-rebuttal recommendation: N/A Justification(s): N/A | N/A Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a well-motivated and elegant, parameter-free framework for online test-time OOD detection in medical vision-language models, effectively addressing both semantic and covariate shifts. In the post-rebuttal phase, the authors comprehensively resolved the core technical critiques by demonstrating robust performance across six distinct base scoring functions and multiple clinical modalities, earning the clear support of the majority of the panel. Although one reviewer maintained a negative recommendation regarding broader impact, the strong empirical gains, thorough validation, and consensus among the other experts lean firmly toward acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents PROTON, a framework for OOD detection with contrastive VLMs that addresses an important limitation of existing works where they focus on semantic shift while ignoring covariate shift, which is highly relevant in medical settings. By incorporating feature-space information through an online-updated memory bank, the method offers a clinically meaningful and technically useful extension. During the review process, reviewers identified an important baseline comparison, which the authors incorporated in the rebuttal. The updated results further demonstrate the strength of the PROTON framework, and reviewers also acknowledged these improvements, shifting toward acceptance. Given the method’s contribution, clinical relevance, and comprehensive analysis, this work represents a solid contribution to MICCAI, and I recommend acceptance. Meta-review #4 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Two reviewers recommend acceptance, and R2 recommends rejection. R2 points out that the proposed method has limited impact beyond the MCM method. R2 also points out limited baselines. However, MCM is usually indeed a strong baseline. Also, the number of comparative methods is limited in the online scenario without training data. Finally, R3 points out the limited experimental evaluations; however, the authors explore various medical VLMs and modalities, which, in my opinion, suffice for a conference version. Based on the above, despite their validity, I do not believe the remaining concerns invalidate the work, which is an interesting, practical contribution to OOD detection using VLMs. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.
